content.chapter: Chapter 1: Introduction & The Creation
objectives: Separate what the chapter presents as true now (Adam’s place as the first Messenger, what the Qur’an does, what we can learn) from the events it narrates in the past.
Explain the role announced for humans on earth (a ruler, khalifah) with the chapter’s own words.
Discover how present and past forms, after + past simple, told/said and would / was going to order time and look forward from a past moment.
Frame the ruler’s role as responsibility rather than unlimited power.
content.pedagogy: The chapter opens with a frame in the present (is, tells, can learn) and then moves into the story in the past. Learners first vote on two board sentences (true now / happened once), then color present and past verbs in the first paragraph and build a three-step timeline: sky and earth → the angels are told → the ruler’s future life on earth. Grammar is discovered from meaning: You ask “Is this still true today, or did it happen once?” and “When the angels heard this, had the ruler’s life on earth started?”, and learners find that would / was going to look forward from a past moment before you name the form.
priorKnowledge: Present simple vs past simple; after as a time linker; the difference between say and tell.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Do not present the ruler’s role as unlimited power, and do not describe the angels as hostile: The chapter says they were surprised and waited with curiosity. Learners may also think every sentence in the first paragraph is present; “Allah created him from soil” is a past event.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: present simple and can for what is true now (is, tells, can learn) vs past simple for story events (created, gave, were) · After + past simple to order two events · tell someone vs say · would / was going to for a future seen from a past moment · a reported earlier decision (He said He had decided …) · began to + base verb.
Notice (Activity 1): learners sort six parts of the chapter into “true now” and “happened in the story”. Ask: “Is this still true today, or did it happen once?” Then ask why “Allah created him from soil” is past although it stands in the present-tense paragraph (it is an event, not a present fact).
Build (Activities 2–3): Complete “… Allah created the sky and the earth, He … the angels that He was going to create a human. … This ruler … live there for many years.” with After / told / would, then fix “He said He has decided …” and “began wait”. After each item ask: “When the angels were told, had the ruler’s life on earth started yet?”
Likely errors: *He said the angels · *will live in a story told in the past · *He said He has decided · *began wait / began to waiting.
Use (Activity 4): four connected sentences that start with a present fact about a source (a book, a museum, a family story), move into past narration with after, and end with was going to or would.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Chunk the announcement with two short pauses: “AFter alLAH creATed the SKY and the EARTH, | He TOLD the ANgels | that He was GOing to creATE a HUman.”
Weak forms: “was” /wəz/, “to” /tə/ in “going to”, “that” /ðət/, “would” /wəd/ in “This RUler would LIVE there …”.
-ed endings: created /ɪd/, decided /ɪd/, showed /d/, surprised /d/.
Contrastive stress in the first paragraph: “this FABulous but TRUE story”.
Word focus: MES-sen-ger, FAB-u-lous, NU-mer-ous, cu-ri-OS-i-ty, GRAND-chil-dren.
beforeReading: Write two sentences on the board: “Our school library has three thousand books.” / “Our school library opened last year.” Learners raise one hand for “true now” and two hands for “happened once”, then name the verb that decided. Ask them to predict: Will the chapter begin with “is” sentences or with “was / did” sentences?
duringReading: First listening, books closed: What does Allah tell the angels?
Second reading: Mark present verbs in the first paragraph in one color and past verbs in another.
Draw a three-step timeline: Sky and earth created → angels told → the ruler’s life on earth.
Underline “was going to” and “would” and write “still in the future then” next to them.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the timeline in view.
Language Focus: Sort present and past (Activity 1), then order, report and look forward (Activities 2–3).
Write four connected sentences about a source you know (a book, a museum, a family story) following the Activity 4 route.
Say in one sentence what “ruler” means if it is a responsibility and not only power (see the Word Note).
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook: Two board sentences (true now / happened once), learners vote with their hands and name the verb that decided; 5–13 Listen with books closed (What does Allah tell the angels?), then read along and color present and past verbs in the first paragraph; 13–19 Pairs draw the three-step timeline and add “would live there for many years” as an arrow into the future, then check the meaning of the role with the Responsibility on Earth hotspot and the Word Note “ruler”; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–32 Language Focus: Activity 1 as a whole-class sort with the question “still true or happened once?”, Activities 2–3 in pairs with a quick board check of said / told; 32–38 Use: Four sentences about a source (a history book, a museum, a family photo) moving from present to past to would, two pairs read aloud and the class names each time shift; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Which sentences are true now, and which tell events inside the story?
From which past moment do “was going to” and “would” look forward?
What in the chapter and in the Word Note “ruler” shows that the role is a responsibility?
interactiveTips: Use the Soil hotspot with “Allah created him from soil” and the Responsibility on Earth hotspot with the announcement of the ruler (khalifah).
Replay the second paragraph and ask learners to raise a hand when they hear “was going to” and again at “would”.
Keep the angels’ reaction exactly as the chapter states it: Surprised and waiting with curiosity.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give a two-column chart (true now / happened then) with the first item done, and the frames “After ____, ____.” and “He told ____ that ____ was going to ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write six connected sentences about a real source that move from present to past, include one reported earlier decision (said that … had decided …) and end with would.

formativeAssessment: Sorts present facts and past events and gives the reason.
Orders events with after and uses told / said correctly.
Uses would / was going to for a future seen from the past.
expectedResponses: The chapter presents Adam (pbuh) in the present as the first Messenger and the father of all humans; in the past it narrates that Allah created him from soil and told the angels He was going to create a human, a ruler who would live on earth for many years.
content.transferTask: Describe a past plan in your school or family: What was decided, and what was going to happen next.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners explain why the tense changes before I named the rule, and did the ruler’s role stay a responsibility rather than power?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, draw a timeline with three steps from the chapter. Add “would live there for many years” as an arrow into the future. Then check the word “ruler” in the Word Note.
checkQuestions: Where does the “would” sentence go on the timeline? (as an arrow into the future)
How many steps do you draw? (three)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Listen for pairs who place “would live” in the past box and ask them “Had it happened yet when Allah spoke?”. In the Use task, note whether learners move from present to past to would. Pick two pairs whose time shifts are clear to read aloud.

exitTicket: Write one sentence that is true now about a book you know and one sentence with “was going to” about a past plan.

rubricLevels.secure: Sorts present facts and past events and says why.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Is this still true today, or did it happen once?” for each sentence.

rubricLevels.secure: Orders the events with after and uses told and said correctly.
rubricLevels.notYet: Write “told + person” and “said + words” on the board and let the learner choose.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses would or was going to for a future seen from the past.
rubricLevels.notYet: Underline “would live” in the text and ask what time it points to.

rubricLevels.secure: Describes the ruler’s role as responsibility, not power.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “What must a good ruler look after?”.

interculturalFocus.notice: The chapter gives humans the role of khalifah, a ruler and caretaker on earth. English has no single word for it, so the Word Note uses 'ruler'.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: What does 'ruler' mean in English and what does 'halife' mean in Turkish? Which word in each language is closer to 'someone who takes care of something for another'?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Translation is never exact. Learners notice that a word can carry a duty in one language and only power in another, and they choose the best English phrase with a reason.

content.chapter: Chapter 2: The Shaping of Adam
objectives: Explain the chapter’s two cause–result links: Soil from different parts of the earth → different skin colors, and life and intellect → learning and understanding.
Follow the order in Allah’s instruction to the angels (creation, life and knowledge first, then respect) and the later gift of knowledge.
Discover how after + present perfect, to + verb, later, more … than and That’s why / because / so show order, purpose, comparison and cause.
Turn respect for human diversity into an observable classroom action.
content.pedagogy: Learners fill three evidence rows on the board (Why different skin colors? / Why life and intellect? / What did Adam receive later?), each with a quoted phrase. The Language Focus then starts from a question of order, not from a rule: “When were the angels to show respect?” Learners discover that “After I have created …” names an action that must be complete first. Finally they turn “That’s why” into “because” and “so” and see that the same cause can be told in either order.
priorKnowledge: Because and so; simple comparatives; purpose with to.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The chapter explains different skin colors by where the soil came from; it does not rank colors. Knowledge is not only memorised facts: Allah taught Adam “everything he needed to do good on earth”.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: After + have/has + past participle for an action that must be complete first · to + base verb for purpose · Later for the next stage · more … than · a reason followed by That’s why, and the same link with because (result first) or so (reason first).
Notice (Activity 1): “After I have created Adam (pbuh) and given him life and knowledge, show respect to him.” Ask only: “What must happen first? What comes second?” Learners find that the instruction waits for a completed action before you name the form.
Build (Activities 2–3): Complete “Allah gave Adam (pbuh) life and intellect … learn and understand. …, He taught Adam (pbuh) everything he needed to do good on earth. He gave Adam (pbuh) more knowledge … the angels.” with to / Later / than, then rewrite the That’s why sentence with because and with so.
Likely errors: *for learn · *more knowledge as the angels · *Humans have different skin colors so … (so placed before the reason) · *because of + a full clause.
Use (Activity 4): four connected sentences about a new learning situation: What a teacher said, why a learner received a tool, the result, and one comparison.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Pause before the result link: “… and alLAH SHAPED ADam. | THAT’S why HUmans have DIFferent SKIN colors.”
Say the instruction in two parts: “AFter I have creATed ADam … | SHOW reSPECT to him.” — “have” is weak (/əv/).
Comparison: “MORE KNOWLedge than the ANgels” — “than” is weak (/ðən/).
-ed endings: collected /ɪd/, shaped /t/, needed /ɪd/.
Word focus: IN-tel-lect, KNOWL-edge (/ˈnɒlɪdʒ/, silent k), HAND-ful, un-der-STAND, DIF-fer-ent.
beforeReading: Show the Different Lands hotspot image and ask pairs to predict in one sentence what soil from many places might explain in the chapter. Keep two predictions on the board to check.
duringReading: First listening: What is the reason for different skin colors?
Fill the three evidence rows with quoted phrases.
Underline Allah’s words to the angels and number the two steps (first … then …).
Circle That’s why, so, to, Later and than.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the evidence rows visible.
Language Focus: Discover the order in Allah’s words (Activity 1), complete purpose, sequence and comparison (Activity 2), then say the same cause in a different order (Activity 3).
Write four sentences about a new learning situation with one reason–result link and one comparison.
Name one respectful action towards classmates who look or speak differently.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: The Different Lands hotspot image, pairs predict what the soil will explain; 4–12 Listen and read, then pairs copy one quoted phrase into each of the three evidence rows; 12–18 Order cards in pairs: Soil collected / Adam shaped / life and knowledge given / respect ordered, learners justify the last card with “After I have created …”; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (What must happen first?), Activity 2 in pairs, Activity 3 on paper, learners hold up their because and so versions; 31–38 Use: Four sentences about a new learning situation (a new tool, a new club), a partner underlines every linker; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Which phrase gives the reason for different skin colors, and which phrase gives the result?
According to Allah’s words, what must be complete before the angels show respect?
Why does the chapter explain difference without ranking one color above another?
interactiveTips: Use the Different Lands hotspot for the soil–color link and the Knowledge and Intellect hotspot for the purpose of life and intellect.
Replay Allah’s words to the angels and ask learners to raise one finger at the first action and two fingers at the instruction.
In the Quick Challenge, ask for the exact linking word (That’s why, so, to, than) before accepting an answer.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Frames: “Humans have different skin colors because ____.”, “Allah gave Adam life and intellect to ____.”, “He gave Adam more ____ than ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write the That’s why sentence in three versions (That’s why / because / so) and explain in one sentence which version puts the result first.

formativeAssessment: Keeps the two cause–result links separate.
Uses to + verb for purpose and more … than correctly.
Rewrites a reason–result link with because and so without changing the meaning.
expectedResponses: Allah’s angels collected soil from different parts of the earth, so humans have different skin colors; Allah gave Adam life and intellect to learn and understand, later taught him everything he needed to do good on earth, and gave him more knowledge than the angels.
content.transferTask: Explain one way your class can show respect to people from different places, using one reason and one result.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners discover the order in “After I have created …” before I named the form, and did the diversity discussion stay respectful and text-based?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, copy one quoted phrase into each of the three evidence rows. Then put the four cards in order and use “After I have created …” to explain the last card.
checkQuestions: Do you copy or rewrite the phrases? (copy them)
Which sentence explains the last card? (After I have created …)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that pairs keep the two links apart: soil from different lands leads to skin colors, and knowledge leads to respect. During Activity 3, look at the held-up because and so versions for meaning changes. Ask one pair with a correct version to explain it.

exitTicket: Write the chapter’s reason for different skin colors twice: once with “That’s why” and once with “because”.

rubricLevels.secure: Keeps the soil–skin color and knowledge–respect links separate.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the two causes on cards and let the learner match the results.

rubricLevels.secure: Orders the events and uses to + verb for purpose.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Why did Allah give him intellect?” and accept “to learn and understand”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses more … than correctly.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “He gave Adam more … than …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Talks about difference with respect and without ranking.
rubricLevels.notYet: Remind the learner of the chapter sentence and ask for one respectful sentence.

interculturalFocus.notice: Soil from different parts of the earth gives different skin colors, and the chapter explains difference without ranking.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Which English words for skin color and origin are polite today, and which are old or offensive? Is it the same in Turkish?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Language about people changes with time. Teach the polite forms and explain that learners should use the name a group uses for itself.

content.chapter: Chapter 3: Iblis’s Arrogance
objectives: Separate the characters’ views (thought, believed, said) from the narrator’s own statements.
Explain Iblis’s criterion for superiority (his origin: fire, not soil) and why the chapter rejects it.
Discover how thought / believed that, more … than, superior to, However, but and “, which made …” build a viewpoint and its answer.
Connect humility with checking an opinion against evidence.
content.pedagogy: The chapter has two voices: The characters and the narrator. While you read eight sentences aloud, learners hold up C (character) or N (narrator) cards; the Language Focus sort then confirms what they found: thought / believed / said mark an opinion that belongs to someone, and the narrator can report it without agreeing (“Iblis was arrogant”, “was wrong about Adam”). Comparison is treated as part of an argument: Iblis compares origins, the narrator answers with “However, in the sight of Allah …”.
priorKnowledge: Think that / believe; comparatives with -er and more; because; but.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The story does not accept that fire is better than soil; Iblis’s words in quotation marks are his claim. The chapter rejects race, color or group membership as the measure of greatness.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: reporting a view (thought that, believed, said) vs the narrator’s statements · comparatives with long adjectives (more important and more valuable than) · superior to (not than) · However for a contrasting view, but inside one sentence · the reported belief stays past (Iblis thought that Adam was …) · “, which made …” for a comment on the whole idea.
Notice (Activity 1): learners sort six parts into “a character’s view” and “the narrator’s own statement”. Ask: “Does the narrator agree with Iblis? Which words tell you that the idea belongs to him?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose more important / to / However in “He thought he was more important and more valuable than Adam (pbuh) …”, “According to Satan, fire was superior to clay.” and “However, in the sight of Allah, …”, then fix “Adam is”, “and Iblis” and “what made”. After each item ask: “Whose view is this sentence now?”
Likely errors: *importanter · *superior than · So instead of However · *Iblis thought that Adam is … · *what made / that made after a comma.
Use (Activity 4): four connected sentences about a new situation with two different opinions, a reason, a comparison and a contrasting conclusion.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Contrastive stress in Iblis’s claim, read calmly as a reported claim: “I am BETter than ADam (pbuh). | You created ME from FIRE, | and You created ADam (pbuh) from SOIL.”
A clear pause and fall-rise on “HOWever, | in the SIGHT of alLAH, | …”.
Comparatives: “MORE imPORtant and MORE VALuable than …” — “than” is weak (/ðən/).
-ed endings: admired /d/, created /ɪd/, believed /d/.
Word focus: AR-ro-gant, su-PE-ri-or, su-pe-ri-OR-i-ty, OR-i-gin, ad-MIRED.
beforeReading: Board two sentences: “Ali thinks that his team is the best.” / “Ali’s team won the match.” Ask which one is Ali’s view and which one the writer tells us as a fact, and which words show the difference (thinks that).
duringReading: First listening: Who does not respect Adam, and what reason does he give?
Color character views (thought / believed / said) and narrator statements differently.
Box Iblis’s comparison (fire / soil) and the narrator’s “However …” answer.
Underline what Iblis could not see and accept.
afterReading: Quick Challenge: For every answer, say whose view it is.
Language Focus: Sort the voices (Activity 1), compare and contrast (Activity 2), then correct the reported belief, the contrast and the which-clause (Activity 3).
Write four sentences about two different opinions on a school question and end with an evidence-based conclusion.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook: “thinks that” vs fact on the board, learners name the signal words; 5–12 Listen and read, then a voice check: You read eight sentences, learners hold up C or N cards; 12–19 Argument map in pairs: Iblis’s claim → his reason (origin) → what he could not see (Adam’s perfect knowledge) → the narrator’s However, each box with a quoted phrase; 19–23 Quick Challenge with speaker ownership; 23–32 Language Focus: Activity 1 whole class (Does the narrator agree?), Activities 2–3 in pairs, then two errors analysed on the board; 32–38 Use: Four sentences about a neutral disagreement (which club is better, which route to school is faster) with thought that, because, more … than and however; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What criterion does Iblis use to decide who is better?
Which sentences show that the narrator does not share his view?
According to the chapter, what does greatness not come from?
How does humility change the way we react to evidence that we are wrong?
interactiveTips: Use the Fire and Soil hotspot for Iblis’s comparison and the Arrogance hotspot for the narrator’s judgement.
Replay “Iblis said, …” and “Iblis was arrogant.” back to back and ask whose voice each one is.
Do not accept “Fire was superior to clay.” in an answer without “According to Satan” or “Iblis believed that”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: A two-column voice chart and the frame “Iblis believed that ____ because ____. However, the chapter says that ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write six sentences reporting two opinions on a neutral question, with one comment clause (“, which made …”) and a However conclusion based on evidence.

formativeAssessment: Attributes each view to the right voice.
Uses more … than and superior to accurately.
States the chapter’s conclusion with However.
expectedResponses: Iblis believed he was better because he was created from fire, but the narrator says he was arrogant and wrong: Adam had perfect knowledge, which made him more valuable, and in the sight of Allah greatness did not come from race, color or group.
content.transferTask: Report two opinions about a neutral school question and add a contrasting conclusion based on evidence.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners keep the character’s view and the narrator’s statement apart without my prompting?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, build the argument map: Iblis’s claim, his reason, what he could not see, and the narrator’s However. Put a quoted phrase in every box.
checkQuestions: How many boxes? (four)
What goes in the last box? (the narrator’s However sentence)
classroomManagement.monitoring: During the C or N card check, watch who hesitates on narrator sentences and sit near them for the map. Listen in the Use task for “However” at the start of a sentence. Write the two board errors from what you hear, not from the book.

rubricLevels.secure: Says which voice owns each sentence, Iblis or the narrator.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Who says this? Does the narrator agree?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses more … than and superior to accurately.
rubricLevels.notYet: Show “superior to” and “better than” side by side.

rubricLevels.secure: States the chapter’s conclusion with However.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “Iblis believed …. However, …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Judges a disagreement without saying one person is worth less.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Can both people still be respected?”.

interculturalFocus.notice: Iblis judges himself by his origin (fire, not soil). The chapter says greatness does not come from origin.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Is 'Where are you from?' a friendly question in Türkiye? In some English-speaking countries it can feel rude if asked again and again to someone born there. Why?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners practise a friendly follow-up instead ('What do you like about your town?'). Do not use any real nationality as an example of arrogance.

content.chapter: Chapter 4: The Expulsion of Iblis
objectives: Trace the chain: Iblis continues his claim → he is sent away → anger and hatred → blame → waiting for a chance → Allah’s warning to Adam.
Distinguish blaming someone else from taking responsibility.
Discover how the past perfect (had put), continued + -ing, want + person + to, because of + noun, wait for a chance to and keep + person + away from show order, persistence, wishes and plans.
Explain why the warning at the end of the chapter matters later in the story.
content.pedagogy: Draw a two-moment timeline on the board: (A) Allah sends Iblis away, (B) Iblis thinks about it and blames Adam. Learners place “had put” under A and “He thought” under B and so discover the past perfect before you name it. Groups then order six chain cards, each backed by a quoted phrase, and mark where blame enters and where the warning comes. The chapter’s verb patterns are rebuilt from chunk cards before the screen activity.
priorKnowledge: Chapter 3: Iblis’s view and the narrator’s judgement; past simple; because.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Iblis does not admit he is wrong; he continues his claim and blames Adam. Adam is not left without help: Allah tells him that Iblis is his enemy and warns him.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: past perfect for the earlier of two past events (He thought that … Allah had put him far from His help) · continued + -ing · want + person + to + verb · because of + noun vs because + clause · wait for a chance to + verb · keep + person + away from · warned + person + to be careful of.
Notice (Activity 1): “He thought that because of Adam (pbuh), Allah had put him far from His help.” Ask: “What happened first: Allah’s ‘Go away!’ or Iblis’s thought? Which verb shows it?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose saying / to be / because of in “But Iblis continued saying he was right …”, “He didn’t want Allah to be kind to Adam (pbuh).” and “He thought that because of Adam (pbuh), …”, then rebuild “He waited for a chance to keep Adam (pbuh) away from Allah’s kindness, just as he himself was.” from chunks.
Likely errors: *continued say · *He didn’t want that Allah is kind · *because Adam · *keep away Adam from.
Use (Activity 4): four sentences about a new situation in which someone continues a harmful plan and another person gives a warning.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Keep verb patterns as chunks: “conTINued SAYing”, “didn’t WANT alLAH to be KIND”, “WAITed for a CHANCE | to KEEP ADam (pbuh) aWAY from …”.
Weak forms: “had” in “had PUT” (/həd/), “to” (/tə/), “of” (/əv/) in “CAREful of”.
-ed endings: continued /d/, hated /ɪd/, waited /ɪd/, warned /d/.
Read Allah’s words “Go away! …” as reported speech in a calm, steady voice, not as a shout.
Word focus: cre-A-tor, EN-e-my, CARE-ful, KIND-ness, ex-PUL-sion.
beforeReading: Retrieve Chapter 3 in one minute: What did Iblis believe, and was he right? Then ask learners to predict: Will Iblis change his mind or continue? Keep the prediction on the board.
duringReading: Listen: Was the prediction right? Which word tells you (continued)?
Number the stages: Continues his claim → sent away → angry and hating → blames Adam → waits for a chance → Adam is warned.
Underline “had put” and label it “earlier”.
Box the warning and the enemy it names.
afterReading: Quick Challenge using the numbered chain.
Language Focus: Discover the order of the two past events (Activity 1), choose the verb patterns (Activity 2) and rebuild Iblis’s plan (Activity 3).
Compare blame and responsibility in a neutral example (a lost football, a broken project) in four sentences that end with a warning.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Retrieval and prediction: Did Iblis accept he was wrong, will he continue?; 5–12 Listen and read, check the prediction with the word “continued”; 12–19 Chain cards in groups of three: Six stages to order, each card backed by a quoted phrase, groups mark where blame enters and where the warning comes; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–32 Language Focus: Activity 1 as discovery with the two-moment timeline on the board, Activity 2 in pairs, Activity 3 first with chunk cards on the desk, then on screen; 32–38 Use: blame vs responsibility in a neutral scenario, four sentences with continued + -ing, because of and warned … to be careful of; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Which word shows that Iblis did not change his mind?
Why is “because of Adam (pbuh)” blame rather than responsibility?
What does Iblis wait for, and what does Allah warn Adam about?
interactiveTips: Use the Distance from Mercy hotspot with “Go away! You are far from My love and care.” and The Warning hotspot with the last sentence of the chapter.
Replay the first paragraph and ask learners to raise a hand when they hear the earlier event (had put).
Keep Iblis’s words and plans reported; never role-play them.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Six ordered chain cards with one gap each and the frames “Iblis continued ____ing.”, “He blamed Adam: because of ____, …”, “Allah warned Adam to be careful of ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a six-sentence analysis of the chain using had + past participle, continued + -ing, because of and keep … away from, and explain the difference between blame and responsibility.

formativeAssessment: Orders the stages and places the warning at the end.
Explains why “had put” is used.
Uses continued + -ing, want + person + to and keep … away from accurately.
expectedResponses: Iblis continued saying he was right, was sent away, got angry with Adam, hated him and blamed him; he waited for a chance to keep Adam away from Allah’s kindness, and Allah told Adam that Iblis was his enemy and warned him to be careful of Iblis.
content.transferTask: Write a neutral scenario in which someone blames another person and someone else gives a responsible warning.
content.teacherReflection: Did the two-moment timeline help learners find the meaning of “had put” themselves, and did they see blame as the opposite of responsibility?

classroomManagement.instructions: In groups of three, put the six chain cards in order. Back each card with a quoted phrase. Mark where blame starts and where the warning comes.
checkQuestions: What do you mark on the chain? (where blame starts and where the warning comes)
Does every card need a phrase from the text? (yes)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Give each group member one job: reader, card holder, checker. Check that the warning to be careful of Iblis is at the end of the chain. Listen for “had put” in the class discussion and ask one group why the earlier past is needed.

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “had + past participle” and one warning with “warned … to be careful of”.

rubricLevels.secure: Orders the stages and puts the warning at the end.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the first and last cards.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains why “had put” shows the earlier event.
rubricLevels.notYet: Draw the two-moment timeline and ask which came first.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses continued + -ing, want + person + to and keep … away from.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give one gap sentence for each pattern.

rubricLevels.secure: Tells blame and taking responsibility apart in a school situation.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Who says sorry in this situation? Who blames others?”.

interculturalFocus.notice: Iblis blames Adam ('because of Adam') instead of himself. Blame and responsibility appear in every culture's sayings.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Which Turkish saying fits blaming others ('Kendi kusurunu görmeyen...')? Which English expression fits ('to pass the buck', 'It's not my fault')?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Sayings carry cultural values. Learners explain one saying in plain English so that a visitor who does not know Turkish could understand it.

content.chapter: Chapter 5: Life in Paradise and the Warning
objectives: Identify the one restriction among all the blessings of Paradise.
Keep Iblis’s promise attributed to him and marked as a lie, as the chapter does.
Discover what called, to be + role, more … than we can imagine and pretending to be mean, and how start / begin, ask … not to and a reported if … would work.
Explain why a friendly-sounding claim needs checking.
content.pedagogy: Establish the exact boundary first: Learners list the blessings and the single restriction in a T-chart. Then a “claim check” line: What Iblis said / what the narrator says (It was a big lie.). In the Language Focus learners discover the reported/direct change themselves by asking “What would Iblis have said in his own words?”: they → you, ate → eat, would → will.
priorKnowledge: Start / begin + verb; negative instructions (Don’t …); first conditional (If …, … will …).
anticipatedMisconceptions: There is only one restriction, and the promise “they would never die” is Iblis’s claim, which the chapter calls a big lie. Iblis only pretends to be their friend.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: meaning of key phrases (a wife called Eve (Hawwa), to be his companion, more wonderful than we can imagine, pretending to be their friend, whispered) · start / begin + to + verb or -ing · ask + person + not to + verb · a reported condition (if they ate …, they would never die) vs the speaker’s direct words (If you eat …, you will never die).
Notice (Activity 1): learners match five phrases with their meanings. Then ask: “Was Iblis really their friend? Which sentence in the chapter tells you?” (It was a big lie.)
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose to feel / living / not to go in “Adam was in Paradise, but he started to feel lonely.”, “They began living in Paradise.” and “Allah only asked them not to go near one tree.”, then turn “He whispered to them that if they ate from that one tree, they would never die.” into Iblis’s direct words.
Likely errors: *started feel · *began to living · *asked them don’t go · *If you will eat · keeping would in the direct words.
Use (Activity 4): four sentences about a new situation with a beginning, one clear rule and a conditional claim that must be checked.
content.pronunciationFocus:
The restriction as one chunk with stress on the negative: “alLAH ONly ASKED them | NOT to GO NEAR | ONE TREE”.
The reported claim with a pause after the if-clause, in a neutral voice: “if they ATE from that ONE TREE, | they would NEVer DIE”.
Comparative: “MORE WONderful than we can iMAGine” — “than” and “can” are weak.
-ed endings: asked /t/, whispered /d/, started /ɪd/.
Word focus: PAR-a-dise, com-PAN-ion, BLESS-ings, pre-TEND-ing, LONE-ly.
beforeReading: Ask: “If a place has hundreds of good things and one rule, what do people usually talk about — the good things or the rule?” Then learners predict: Will the chapter have one rule or many?
duringReading: Listen with books closed: How many rules does Allah give?
T-chart: blessings / the one restriction.
Underline how Iblis comes near them (pretending to be their friend) and the narrator’s comment (It was a big lie.).
Label the if-sentence “Iblis’s claim”.
afterReading: Quick Challenge: Check the one restriction and who made the promise.
Language Focus: Match the phrases (Activity 1), choose the verb patterns (Activity 2), then turn the reported claim into direct words (Activity 3).
Write four sentences about a new situation (a club, a school trip) with a beginning, one rule and a claim that needs checking.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook: The “many good things, one rule” question and a class prediction; 5–12 Listen with books closed (how many rules?), then read along; 12–18 T-chart in pairs: blessings / the one restriction, then a claim-check line under it: What Iblis said / what the narrator says; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 in pairs with the follow-up (Was Iblis really their friend?), Activity 2 individually, Activity 3 as whole-class discovery of what changes when Iblis speaks himself (they → you, ate → eat, would → will); 31–38 Use: Four sentences about a new place with one rule and a friendly-sounding claim, partners add one question that would check the claim; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: How many restrictions are stated, and how many blessings?
What does “pretending to be their friend” tell us before Iblis even speaks?
Why must “they would never die” stay attributed to Iblis?
interactiveTips: Use the Life in Paradise hotspot for the blessings and The One Tree hotspot for the single restriction.
Replay “It was a big lie.” right after “pretending to be their friend”.
Correct any Quick Challenge explanation that turns Iblis’s promise into a fact.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Frames: “They were asked not to ____.”, “He pretended to be ____.”, “He said that if ____, they would ____. It was a lie.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write six sentences about a new situation: A beginning (started to …), a comparison (more … than), a negative request (asked … not to …), a reported claim with if … would, and the same claim as direct words.

formativeAssessment: States the single restriction accurately.
Keeps the claim attributed and identifies it as a lie.
Changes a reported if … would sentence into direct words.
expectedResponses: Adam started to feel lonely, and Allah gave him Eve to be his companion; all the blessings of Paradise were for them and Allah only asked them not to go near one tree, but Iblis, pretending to be their friend, whispered that if they ate from that tree they would never die, which was a big lie.
content.transferTask: Write a neutral claim with “If … will …”, report it with “said that if … would …”, and add one question that checks it.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners discover the reported/direct change themselves, and did the promise stay labelled as Iblis’s lie?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, make a T-chart: the blessings of Paradise on one side, the one restriction on the other. Under it, write what Iblis said and what the narrator says.
checkQuestions: How many restrictions are there? (one)
Who said that they would never die? (Iblis)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that pairs write only one restriction. In Activity 3, listen for the changes they → you, ate → eat, would → will. In the Use task, check that each pair adds a question that tests the claim.

exitTicket: Write “He said that if ____, ____ would ____.” and the same claim as direct words.

rubricLevels.secure: States the single restriction accurately.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “How many trees did Allah tell them not to go near?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Keeps the claim with Iblis and calls it a lie.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Who said this? What does the narrator call it?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses start to, give … to be and ask … not to correctly.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give one example of each pattern from the text to copy.

rubricLevels.secure: Changes the reported if … would sentence into Iblis’s direct words.
rubricLevels.notYet: Show the three changes on the board as a model.

interculturalFocus.notice: Paradise is a place of blessings with one restriction. Pictures of Paradise as a garden appear in many cultures, and 'paradise' comes from an old Persian word for a walled garden.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: How do Turkish homes, mosques and palaces use gardens and water (Topkapı, Ottoman courtyard fountains)? How are gardens used in an English town (public parks, allotments)?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Keep the comparison on gardens and places, not on beliefs. Learners compare one detail they actually know.

content.chapter: Chapter 6: Satan’s Lies and Adam’s Departure from Paradise
objectives: Order the events: trick → forgotten warning → eating → feelings → discovery → covering.
Explain what “eventually” and “managed to” say together about Iblis’s effort.
Discover the past perfect (the warning Allah had given them), a chain of past simple actions, when-clauses, and so / to / because for result, purpose and reason.
Keep the explanation of modesty (haya) within the chapter’s own words.
content.pedagogy: The warning from Chapter 4 goes above an empty timeline; learners stick six event strips under it and read the order aloud. “Had given” is linked with an arrow to the warning above the line, so learners see why it is earlier. In the Language Focus they first decide “Was it easy for Iblis? Did he succeed?” and find that “eventually” and “managed to” answer both questions, then label so / to / because as result, purpose and reason. The last paragraph is read once, calmly and briefly.
priorKnowledge: Chapter 4 warning; past simple; so and because; to + verb for purpose.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “Managed to” does not mean that tricking them was easy. Do not add detail to the last paragraph or turn the chapter’s explanation of haya into a general rule of your own.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: Eventually + managed to (success after effort) · convinced + person + to + verb · past perfect for the earlier warning (the warning Allah had given them) · a chain of past simple actions (stretched out, picked, offered) · When + past simple for a turning point · so (result) / to + verb (purpose) / because + clause (reason).
Notice (Activity 1): “Eventually, Iblis managed to trick them.” Ask: “Was it easy for Iblis? Did he succeed? Which two words tell you?” Then point to “the warning Allah had given them”: which came first, the warning or the forgetting?
Build (Activities 2–3): Put five parts of the chapter in order using the verbs and “When Adam finished eating, …”, then complete “… had no clothes on, so they both started cutting tree leaves in Paradise to cover themselves. They hurried to hide their private parts because …”.
Likely errors: *managed tricking · *convinced them believe · *for cover themselves · *because of + a full clause.
Use (Activity 4): four sentences about a new situation in which an earlier warning is forgotten, an action changes something and someone reacts for a clear purpose.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Success after effort: “eVENtually, | IBlis MANaged to TRICK them.”
The action chain with an even rhythm and small pauses: “ADam STRETCHED OUT his HAND, | PICKED one of the FRUITS | and OFfered it to EVE.”
-ed endings: tricked /t/, convinced /t/, stretched /t/, picked /t/, offered /d/, changed /d/, ceased /t/, hurried /d/.
Read the last paragraph quietly and factually, without lingering.
Word focus: e-VEN-tu-al-ly, for-BID-den, AT-mos-phere, HAR-mo-ny, VIS-i-ble, sur-ROUND-ing.
beforeReading: Recall the warning from Chapter 4 (Allah warned Adam to be careful of Iblis) and write it above an empty timeline. Ask: “What could make someone forget a warning?”
duringReading: Listen: Which word tells us that Iblis finally succeeded?
Add the events to the timeline under the warning.
Circle “had given” and connect it with an arrow to the warning above the line.
Label so / to / because in the last paragraph as RESULT / PURPOSE / REASON.
afterReading: Quick Challenge from the timeline.
Language Focus: discover “eventually” + “managed to” (Activity 1), order the events (Activity 2), then choose so / to / because (Activity 3).
Write four connected sentences about a neutral forgotten-warning situation (a safety rule in the science lab, a missed deadline).
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Retrieve the Chapter 4 warning and place it above an empty timeline on the board; 5–12 Listen and read, then learners say which word shows that Iblis finally succeeded; 12–18 Strip sequencing in pairs: Six event strips (trick, forget, eat, feel, discover, cover) stuck under the warning and read aloud in order; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (easy or difficult, success or not?), Activity 2 as a check of the strip order, Activity 3 in pairs with the labels result / purpose / reason; 31–38 Use: A neutral consequence chain (a forgotten warning on a school trip or in the science lab), four sentences with managed to, when, so and to; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Which event happened before the main events of this chapter, and which verb form shows it?
How do so, to and because do different jobs in the last paragraph?
What reason does the chapter give for covering themselves, and why should we not add more to it?
interactiveTips: Use The Forbidden Tree hotspot for the sequence of actions and the Modesty hotspot for the chapter’s own explanation (haya).
Replay the first paragraph and ask learners to count the past simple actions in the chain.
Keep the discussion of the last paragraph brief and non-graphic, and return to the exact sentence if interpretation grows.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: The six event strips and the frames “Eventually, ____ managed to ____.”, “They ____, so they ____.”, “They ____ to ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write seven sentences about a neutral situation using eventually, managed to, had + past participle, when, so, to and because, and label each linker.

formativeAssessment: Orders the events with the earlier warning above the line.
Explains “eventually” and “managed to” together.
Distinguishes result, purpose and reason.
expectedResponses: Eventually Iblis managed to trick them, and they forgot the warning Allah had given them; Adam picked a fruit and offered it to Eve, they both ate, Adam felt pain, sadness and shame, and when they saw they had no clothes on they cut leaves to cover themselves because a sense of shame (haya) is part of inborn human nature.
content.transferTask: Describe a neutral situation in which an earlier warning is forgotten, and explain the result, the purpose of the reaction and the reason.
content.teacherReflection: Did the timeline keep the earlier warning visible, and did the discussion of modesty stay within the chapter’s words?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, stick the six event strips under the warning on the board. Read them aloud in order.
checkQuestions: Where does the warning go? (above the timeline)
How many strips? (six)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check the order trick, forget, eat, feel, discover, cover. Listen in Activity 3 for the labels result, purpose and reason. In the Use task, keep the scenario neutral and check for managed to.

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “so” (result) and one with “to + verb” (purpose) about the same situation.

rubricLevels.secure: Orders the events with the earlier warning above the line.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the first and last strips.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains eventually and managed to as success after effort.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Was it easy for Iblis? Did he succeed?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Tells result, purpose and reason apart.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give three sentences and three labels to match.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses only the information in the text.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Where does the text say this?”.

interculturalFocus.notice: Adam and Eve feel shame and cover themselves. Ideas of modesty and privacy are shared by many cultures, but they are expressed in different ways.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask a general question only: How do people show respect for privacy in Türkiye (knocking, taking shoes off at the door)? What is a sign of privacy in an English-speaking home (a closed door, asking before visiting)?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Do not ask learners about clothes or bodies. Keep the talk on homes and visiting habits.

content.chapter: Chapter 7: Forgiveness and Repentance
objectives: Compare Adam and Eve’s response to their mistake with Iblis’s response.
Explain repentance through the chapter’s steps: sadness, saying sorry, learning, deciding never to repeat, asking for pardon.
Discover the meaning of the key phrases and how but, On the other hand, because, decide never to, want + person + to and to + verb express intention, contrast and decision.
Apply admit → learn → decide to a small everyday mistake.
content.pedagogy: Learners build two response profiles in columns (Adam and Eve / Iblis), each step with a quoted phrase, and number the steps of repentance in the second paragraph. The Language Focus then asks why the chapter uses “but” inside one sentence and “On the other hand” at the start of a new paragraph: Learners discover that the second one moves the whole text to a contrasting person. Adam’s words at the start are read calmly as reported words; prophets are never acted out.
priorKnowledge: Chapter 6 events; but and because; want to / decide to.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Repentance in the chapter is more than sadness: It includes saying sorry, learning and a decision about the future. Life on earth is not presented only as punishment: Allah pardoned them, taught them and made them rulers of the earth.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: key phrases (it wasn’t on purpose, learned from their mistake, pardon, chose an opposite path, the biggest barrier) · but inside one sentence vs On the other hand between two paths · because + clause · decide never to + verb · want + person + to + verb · to + verb for purpose (put them on earth to live there).
Notice (Activity 1): learners match five phrases with their meanings. Then ask: “Which phrases describe Adam and Eve, and which describe Iblis? What is the biggest difference between them?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Complete “They made a mistake, but it wasn’t on purpose. … On the other hand, Iblis chose an opposite path. He never admitted he was wrong because he was arrogant.”, then choose to repeat / to pardon / to live.
Likely errors: *decided never repeating · *wanted that Allah pardons them · *for live there · but used to open a new paragraph where On the other hand is needed.
Use (Activity 4): four sentences about an unintentional mistake, a responsible response and a useful next step.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Read the opening words calmly as reported words, not as acting: “forGIVEness! forGIVEness!”, “NO, my LORD, | but I am SHY of YOU.”
Contrast: “They made a misTAKE, | but it WASn’t on PURpose.”, then a longer pause and a fresh start for “On the OTHer HAND, | …”.
Decision: “deCIDed NEVer to rePEAT it” — the stress is on NEVer.
Word focus: for-GIVE-ness, re-PENT-ance, PAR-don, BAR-ri-er, dis-TIN-guish-ing, AR-ro-gance.
beforeReading: Offer three responses to a small mistake (a borrowed ruler is broken): hide it / blame someone / admit it and change. Learners vote and give one reason.
duringReading: Listen: What does Adam answer when he is asked “Are you running away from Me?”
Two columns: Adam and Eve / Iblis, each with quoted phrases.
Number the steps of repentance in the second paragraph.
Underline the role given at the end (the rulers of planet Earth).
afterReading: Quick Challenge with evidence from both columns.
Language Focus: Match the phrases (Activity 1), link the two responses (Activity 2), choose the decision, wish and purpose forms (Activity 3).
Write a four-sentence repair plan for a small school mistake with “wasn’t on purpose”, “learned from”, “decided never to” and “on the other hand”.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: Three responses to a small mistake, class vote with a reason; 4–11 Listen and read, then learners say what Adam’s answer shows (he is shy before Allah, not running away); 11–18 Two response profiles in pairs: Five quoted steps for Adam and Eve, two for Iblis, then a whole-class check of the order (sad → sorry → learned → decided → asked for pardon); 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 in pairs with the follow-up (who does each phrase describe?), Activity 2 as discovery of but vs On the other hand, Activity 3 individually; 31–38 Use: A four-sentence repair plan for a neutral school mistake (a lost library book), a partner checks that the plan contains a decision about the future; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What shows that repentance in the chapter is more than feeling sad?
How do the two responses differ, and what reason does the chapter give for Iblis’s path?
What does the chapter call the biggest barrier to acting the right way?
What role do Adam and Eve receive on earth after they are pardoned?
interactiveTips: Use the Mistake and Pardon hotspot for Adam and Eve’s steps and the Arrogance as a Barrier hotspot for Iblis’s path.
Replay the sentence with “On the other hand” and ask what changes in the text at that point.
Do not ask learners to act out Adam’s words; read them calmly as reported speech.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Frames: “It wasn’t on purpose, but ____.”, “I learned from ____ and decided never to ____.”, “On the other hand, ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write six connected sentences comparing two responses to a neutral mistake with but, on the other hand, because, decided never to and wanted + person + to.

formativeAssessment: Names the steps of repentance with evidence.
Uses but and On the other hand for the right kind of contrast.
Uses decide never to, want + person + to and to + verb accurately.
expectedResponses: Adam and Eve made a mistake that wasn’t on purpose; they were very sad, said sorry, learned from it, decided never to repeat it and wanted Allah to pardon them. On the other hand, Iblis never admitted he was wrong because he was arrogant. Allah pardoned Adam and Eve and put them on earth to live there as its rulers.
content.transferTask: Apply admit → learn → decide to a small everyday mistake in four sentences.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners discover the difference between but and On the other hand, and did the repair plans stay small, safe and personal rather than religious claims?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, write five quoted steps for Adam and Eve and two for Iblis. Then check the order with the class.
checkQuestions: How many steps for Adam and Eve? (five)
How many for Iblis? (two)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Listen for the order sad, sorry, learned, decided, asked for pardon. During Activity 2, note who uses On the other hand between two sentences. In the Use task, check that each plan has a decision about the future.

exitTicket: Write one “learned from … and decided never to …” sentence and one “On the other hand, …” sentence.

rubricLevels.secure: Names the repentance steps with evidence and Iblis’s different response.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the steps on cards to put in order.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses but inside a sentence and On the other hand between sentences.
rubricLevels.notYet: Show one example of each from the text.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses decide never to, want + person + to and to + verb.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “I decided never to … because …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Writes a safe repair plan for a neutral school mistake.
rubricLevels.notYet: Offer the lost library book example as a model.

interculturalFocus.notice: Adam and Eve repent: sadness, saying sorry, learning and deciding. Apologies follow similar steps in many languages, but the words differ.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Which English apology phrases match Turkish ones ('Özür dilerim' / 'I apologise'; 'Kusura bakma' / 'I hope you don't mind')? Which phrase is formal and which is informal?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Some cultures expect a very direct apology, others a softer one. Neither is more sincere; learners choose the phrase that fits the person and the situation.

content.chapter: Chapter 8: Struggle and Survival on Earth
objectives: Classify the responsibilities in the chapter: crops and animals, shelter, nature, the weak, protection.
Separate the expected role (would), what was necessary (had to) and what happened (left, arrived, lived).
Discover to + verb and for + noun for purpose, with + noun for means, for + a period for duration, and how would, had to, in addition, both … and and want + person + not to are used.
Distinguish personal survival from wider responsibility for nature and the weak.
content.pedagogy: Three questions go on the board: Why? With what? How long? Learners sort phrases under them and discover that “for” has two jobs (for shelter / for many years). A group action map then turns the chapter into responsibilities with a purpose or a means for each. Finally learners compare the first paragraph (They would …) with the second (they had to …) and decide which describes a role still ahead and which a necessity.
priorKnowledge: Must / have to; purpose with to; because.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The chapter is not only about personal survival: Protecting nature and helping the weak are part of the role. The first paragraph describes what they would do (a role still ahead), not what had already happened.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: to + verb and for + noun for purpose · with + noun for means · for + a period of time for duration · would for an expected role seen from the past · had to for past necessity · In addition · both … and … · want + person + not to + verb.
Notice (Activity 1): learners sort five phrases into Why? / With what? / How long? Ask: “‘for shelter’ and ‘for many years’ both use for. Do they answer the same question?”
Build (Activities 2–3): correct “They will use land …”, “to struggle for survive” and “he wanted people don’t remember Allah”, then complete “In addition, they had to protect themselves with clothes and weapons … They had both good and difficult times …”.
Likely errors: *They will use land (in a past story) · *for survive · *wanted people don’t remember · *they must protect (for the past) · *either good and difficult.
Use (Activity 4): four sentences about people beginning life in a difficult new place.
content.pronunciationFocus:
“had to” is /ˈhæd tə/: practise “they HAD to STRUGgle | to surVIVE”.
Purpose phrases stay with their action: “use LAND | to GROW CROPS | and KEEP ANimals”.
Contrast the two jobs of for: “for SHELter” / “for MAny YEARS”.
Weak forms: “to” /tə/, “and” /ən/, “would” /wəd/.
Word focus: sur-VIVE, STRUG-gle, SHEL-ter, WEAP-ons (/ˈwepənz/), de-SCEN-dants.
beforeReading: Ask pairs: “You arrive in a new, empty place. What three things must you do first?” Collect answers under three headings: survival / nature / people.
duringReading: Listen: Which of our ideas are in the chapter?
Sort each responsibility under survival / nature / people.
Mark would (expected role), had to (necessity) and past simple (what happened) in three colors.
Underline why Iblis was still there.
afterReading: Quick Challenge with the action map.
Language Focus: Sort why / with what / how long (Activity 1), correct would, to survive and wanted people not to (Activity 2), then add In addition / had to / both (Activity 3).
Write a four-sentence responsibility plan for a class project or a school garden.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook: “a new, empty place” brainstorm under survival / nature / people; 5–12 Listen and read, then tick the brainstorm ideas that the chapter mentions; 12–18 Action map in groups of four: Each learner takes one area (survival, nature, the weak, protection), finds the phrase and adds its purpose or means; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 whole class with the “two jobs of for” question, Activities 2–3 in pairs, then learners say which sentences describe what would happen, what had to happen and what did happen; 31–38 Use: A responsibility plan for a school garden or class project (would, had to, to + verb, in addition, with), shown in a short gallery walk; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Which responsibilities go beyond staying alive?
What is the difference between “They would …” and “they had to …” in this chapter?
Why was Iblis still there, according to the chapter?
interactiveTips: Use the Work on Earth hotspot for the expected role and the Struggle and Survival hotspot for the necessities.
Replay the first paragraph and ask “necessary for what?” after each purpose phrase.
Use the Quick Challenge to check the action map, not to test memory of the list.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Responsibility cards and the frames “They had to ____ to ____.”, “In addition, they ____.”, “They protected themselves with ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a seven-sentence plan with would, had to, to + verb, with + noun, for + a period, in addition and both … and.

formativeAssessment: Identifies responsibilities beyond survival.
Separates expected role, necessity and events.
Uses the two meanings of for correctly.
expectedResponses: The chapter first describes the role they would have (grow crops, keep animals, build buildings for shelter, protect nature, help the weak); on earth they had to struggle to survive, work hard and protect themselves with clothes and weapons, and Iblis was still there because he wanted people not to remember Allah.
content.transferTask: Describe four responsibilities in a class project, with a purpose for each.
content.teacherReflection: Did the three questions (Why? With what? How long?) make the forms meaningful, and did responsibility become concrete action?

classroomManagement.instructions: In groups of four, each person takes one area: survival, nature, the weak or protection. Find the phrase in the chapter and add its purpose or means.
checkQuestions: How many areas does each person take? (one)
What do you add after the phrase? (its purpose or means)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that the group covers responsibilities beyond survival, such as protecting nature and helping the weak. Listen for the two uses of for. During the gallery walk, look for would, had to and to + verb in the plans.

exitTicket: Write one “had to … to …” sentence and one “In addition, …” sentence about a class project.

rubricLevels.secure: Names responsibilities beyond survival from the text.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the “protect nature” and “help the weak” phrases.

rubricLevels.secure: Separates the expected role (would), the necessity (had to) and the events.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Is this a plan, a must or something that happened?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses to + verb, with and for for purpose, means and duration.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give one model sentence for each.

rubricLevels.secure: Writes a plan with actions others can see.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “What will people see you do?”.

interculturalFocus.notice: On earth the first family grows crops, raises animals, builds shelter and protects the weak. These are the basic needs of every human culture.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: How do people in Konya protect the weak today (neighbours, kermes, food banks)? What does a charity do in an English-speaking town?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Helping can be private in one culture and public in another. Learners present both as good ways to help, without judging.

content.chapter: Chapter 9: The First Messenger and the Path of Guidance
objectives: Explain how Adam’s role develops when a community forms.
Distinguish a beginning (started teaching) from continuation (never stopped sending).
Discover stop + -ing vs stop + to, the chapter’s time markers, teach + person + to, to + verb for purpose and if + present for a general truth.
Explain guidance as continuing through many messengers who followed the same path.
content.pedagogy: Learners draw a role line (first human → first father → first Messenger who teaches) with a quoted phrase at each step. A time-marker race follows: Pairs match At that time / After a period of time / Thus / Years later with their sentences from memory and check in the text. In the Language Focus learners test two school sentences (I stopped talking / I stopped to talk) and discover why “never stopped sending” means the sending went on.
priorKnowledge: Chapter 8; become; start + -ing; if-sentences with the present simple.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Guidance is not a single event: Allah never stopped sending messengers and sacred texts, and all the messengers followed the same path. “Stopped to send” would change the meaning.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: stop + -ing vs stop + to + verb (Allah never stopped sending messengers …) · time markers (At that time, After a period of time, when …, Thus, Years later, after the death of …) · became for a new role · teach + person + to + verb · to + verb for purpose · if + present simple, present simple for a general truth.
Notice (Activity 1): true or false: “Allah never stopped sending messengers …” has the same meaning as “Allah never stopped to send messengers.” Ask: “Did the sending end? What would ‘stopped to send’ mean?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Order four parts of the chapter with the time markers, then correct “teaching people live”, “for show people the right path” and “if people will forget Allah”.
Likely errors: *never stopped to send · *teaching people live · *for show · *if people will forget.
Use (Activity 4): four sentences about someone who begins guiding a group.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Time markers at the start of a sentence take a short pause: “At THAT TIME, |”, “AFter a PEriod of TIME, |”, “YEARS LAter, |”.
Continuation: “NEVer STOPPED SENDing” — “stopped” is one syllable (/stɒpt/).
General truth: “if PEOple forGET alLAH, | they LOSE the MEANing and PURpose of LIFE”.
Word focus: com-MU-ni-ty, RIGHT-eous-ly (/ˈraɪtʃəsli/), SA-cred, MES-sen-gers, PUR-pose.
beforeReading: Ask: “A group of five friends becomes a class of thirty. What new responsibilities appear?” Collect two answers.
duringReading: Listen: What new role does Adam have when a community forms?
Draw the role line with a quoted phrase at each step.
Circle the time markers.
Underline what Adam and Eve taught their children and why.
afterReading: Quick Challenge with the role line.
Language Focus: Stopped sending vs stopped to send (Activity 1), order with time markers (Activity 2), correct teach … to, the purpose and the general if-clause (Activity 3).
Write four sentences about someone who began guiding a group (a team captain, a club leader) and kept doing it.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: “five friends become thirty” question; 4–11 Listen and read, then the role line on the board with a quoted phrase at each step; 11–18 Time-marker race in pairs: Four time phrases on slips matched with their sentences from memory, then checked in the text; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery with two school sentences (I stopped talking / I stopped to talk), Activity 2 as a check of the race, Activity 3 in pairs; 31–38 Use: A guidance paragraph about a team captain or club leader (when …, became, started teaching … to …, never stopped + -ing), two volunteers read and the class names the time markers; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: How does Adam’s role change when a community forms?
What is the difference between “started teaching” and “never stopped sending”?
According to the chapter, what do people lose if they forget Allah, and what did all the messengers want?
interactiveTips: Use the A Community Forms hotspot for the role change and the Continuing Guidance hotspot for “never stopped sending”.
Replay the second paragraph and ask what Adam and Eve taught their children and why.
Require the role change, not only an event, in Quick Challenge explanations.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: A three-stage role line and the frames “When ____, he became ____.”, “He started teaching people to ____.”, “____ never stopped ____ing.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write six sentences with four time markers, teach + person + to, never stopped + -ing and one general if-sentence.

formativeAssessment: Explains the role change with evidence.
Distinguishes stop + -ing from stop + to.
Uses time markers and teach + person + to correctly.
expectedResponses: When a community formed, Adam became the first Messenger of Allah and started teaching people to live righteously and act honestly; Allah never stopped sending messengers and sacred texts, and years after Adam’s death many messengers followed the same path.
content.transferTask: Describe someone who began guiding a group and never stopped doing it.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners discover the two meanings of stop themselves, and did they see guidance as continuing rather than a single event?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, match the four time phrases to their sentences from memory. Then check them in the text.
checkQuestions: Do you look at the text first? (no, from memory first)
How many time phrases? (four)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Watch the race and note phrases most pairs miss, then go back to them in the class check. Listen for stop + -ing and stop + to in Activity 1. Ask two volunteers to read their guidance paragraph and the class to name the time markers.

exitTicket: Write one “became …” sentence and one “never stopped …ing” sentence about someone you know.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains how Adam became the first Messenger with evidence.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “What happened before he became a Messenger?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Tells stop + -ing from stop + to.
rubricLevels.notYet: Use the two school sentences as a model.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses time markers such as when and years after correctly.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the four markers on cards to place in a paragraph.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses teach + person + to for purpose and the present for a general truth.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “He started teaching people to …”.

interculturalFocus.notice: Adam guides a growing community. Every culture has people who teach and guide others.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Who guides a community in Türkiye (the teacher, the imam, the muhtar, elders)? Who does it in an English-speaking town (a mayor, a teacher, a community leader)?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Roles that look similar may carry different expectations. Learners describe one role in both cultures before they judge which is better.

content.chapter: Chapter 10: The Two Sons: Habil and Qabil
objectives: Describe the two brothers’ character and work with evidence.
Identify the shared obligation (to make an offering) and the different choices.
Discover the meaning of the key phrases and how became, had to, best / healthiest, loved + -ing, but and care about + -ing are used, together with the closing general principle.
Explain goodness through care and effort, not through profession or amount alone.
content.pedagogy: Learners fill profile cards (character, work, gift, attitude) for each brother with quoted phrases, and the class agrees on the one obligation they share. The Language Focus starts from meaning: “Which word makes Qabil’s gift sound small, and what is it contrasted with?” Learners find “just” and “but” before any rule is named, then notice that the last sentence switches to the present (real goodness is giving …) because it states a general principle.
priorKnowledge: Superlatives; had to; but and however.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Do not explain the difference by the brothers’ jobs (shepherd / farmer) or by the amount alone: The chapter points to care and effort (his best and healthiest sheep / just a handful of crops that were not very valuable; didn’t care about pleasing Allah).
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: key phrases (grew up to be, mostly jealous, a serious disagreement, just a handful of) · became (irregular past) · had to for a past obligation · superlatives (best and healthiest, the best and the most loved) · loved + -ing · but for contrast · care about + -ing · a general principle in the present (real goodness is giving out …).
Notice (Activity 1): learners match four phrases with their meanings. Then ask: “Which word makes Qabil’s gift sound small? What is it contrasted with?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose became / had to / best in “When they grew up, Habil became a shepherd.”, “To solve the problem, they had to make an offering to Allah.” and “Habil brought his best and healthiest sheep …”, then fix “loved take care of”, “and Qabil” and “care about please”.
Likely errors: *becomed · must for the past · *most good · *loved take · *care about please.
Use (Activity 4): four sentences about two people who respond differently to the same task, ending with a general principle.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Contrast the two gifts with stress: “HAbil brought his BEST and HEALthiest SHEEP … | but QAbil brought JUST a HANDful of his CROPS”.
The principle is present and general — slow down: “REAL GOODness | is GIVing OUT the BEST | and the MOST LOVED”.
-ed ending in “loved” /d/ (one syllable).
Word focus: JEAL-ous (/ˈdʒeləs/), SHEP-herd (/ˈʃepəd/, silent h), dis-a-GREE-ment, OF-fer-ing, HEALTH-i-est, VAL-u-a-ble.
beforeReading: Neutral example: Two classmates must each bring one item to a charity box; one chooses a good book, one brings a torn page. Ask: “Same task? Same care?”
duringReading: Listen: How are the brothers different?
Profile cards: Habil / Qabil (character, work, gift, attitude).
Underline the shared obligation (had to make an offering).
Box the general principle in the last sentence.
afterReading: Quick Challenge with evidence for both brothers.
Language Focus: Phrase meanings (Activity 1), became / had to / best (Activity 2), then corrections with loved + -ing, but and care about + -ing (Activity 3).
Write four sentences comparing two approaches to the same neutral task and end with a principle.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook: The charity-box example, learners decide what makes a gift valuable; 5–12 Listen and read, then a quick true/false round on the brothers’ work (shepherd / farmer); 12–19 Profile cards in pairs: Four rows for each brother, each with a quoted phrase, then the class agrees on the shared obligation; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 in pairs with the follow-up (Which word makes the gift sound small?), Activities 2–3 individually, then learners explain one correction to a partner; 31–38 Use: Four sentences comparing two approaches to one school task (a group poster) with had to, but and a principle (Real teamwork is …ing); 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What obligation do the brothers share, and why?
What evidence shows that the two gifts differed in care, not only in type?
Why is it not enough to say “Habil was a shepherd, so his gift was better”?
What general principle does the chapter state?
interactiveTips: Use the Two Different Brothers hotspot for character and work and The Two Offerings hotspot for the gifts.
Replay the sentence with “but Qabil brought just a handful …” and ask learners to name the two sides of the contrast.
Attach “had to” to the shared obligation before comparing choices.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Frame: “Both brothers had to ____. Habil brought ____, but Qabil brought ____. Qabil didn’t care about ____ing.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write six sentences separating obligation, action, attitude and principle, with one superlative and one “care about + -ing”.

formativeAssessment: Identifies the shared obligation.
Uses evidence from both brothers.
Uses had to, superlatives and care about + -ing accurately.
expectedResponses: Habil became a shepherd and Qabil was a farmer; to solve their disagreement they had to make an offering, but Habil brought his best and healthiest sheep while Qabil brought just a handful of crops and didn’t care about pleasing Allah and his father. Real goodness is giving out the best and the most loved.
content.transferTask: Compare two approaches to the same neutral task and finish with a principle (Real … is …ing).
content.teacherReflection: Did learners judge the brothers from evidence of care and effort rather than from their jobs?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, complete four rows for each brother. Put a quoted phrase in each row. Then agree as a class on what both brothers had to do.
checkQuestions: How many rows for each brother? (four)
What do we agree on together? (what both brothers had to do)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that the shared obligation, the offering, is not given to one brother only. Listen in Activity 1 for “just a handful” as the words that make the gift small. In the Use task, check that each pair ends with a principle sentence.

exitTicket: Complete: “Both had to ____, but ____. Real ____ is ____ing.”

rubricLevels.secure: States what both brothers had to do.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “What did both of them have to bring?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Gives evidence from both brothers.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask for one phrase from each column.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses but, superlatives and care about + -ing accurately.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “Habil brought his best …, but Qabil …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Writes one general principle such as “Real teamwork is …ing”.
rubricLevels.notYet: Show the chapter sentence about real goodness as a model.

interculturalFocus.notice: The two sons must make an offering. Turkish learners know Kurban; English speakers may know only the word 'sacrifice'.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: How would you explain Kurban Bayramı to an English-speaking friend in three sentences? Which English words are useful (to share meat, neighbours, the poor)?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Explaining your own culture in English is an intercultural skill. Learners avoid saying 'It is just like Christmas' and describe the festival on its own terms.

content.chapter: Chapter 11: The First Conflict and the Raven
objectives: Trace the events calmly: Offering accepted → Qabil’s anger and threat → Habil’s refusal → the killing → sadness and panic → the raven shows the way.
Distinguish a threat (will) from a refusal (won’t) and keep each speaker’s words attributed.

Discover how will / won’t, past simple admissions, present judgments (am worse than, cannot), because, start to, show … the way to and reported speech (admitted that he had killed, did not know what he should do) work.
Develop safe, non-violent steps for stopping an argument.
content.pedagogy: Two lessons. Lesson 1 protects meaning and atmosphere: A class rule (calm reading, no acting), one listening for Habil’s answer, calm event cards and speaker labels, and a close look at threat vs refusal. Lesson 2 starts from the bridge note and opens the language: Learners discover that the only difference between the threat and the refusal is will / won’t, then report Qabil’s words and transfer the language to a neutral situation and to safe prevention steps.
priorKnowledge: Chapter 10: the brothers’ different attitudes; will for the future; reported speech with said that.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Habil does not answer with violence; he refuses. The raven does not cause anything; it shows Qabil the way to put the body in the pit. No re-enactment and no added graphic detail.
content.grammarFocus:
