Targets: will for a threat vs won’t for a refusal · past simple to admit finished actions (I killed, I did) · present for a judgment or inability (I am worse than this raven, I cannot hide …) · worst vs worse than · because + clause vs because of + noun · start + to + verb · show + person + the way to + verb · reporting an admission and a question (admitted that he had killed, did not know what he should do / what to do).
Notice (Activity 1): learners sort six spoken sentences into the future, the past and now. Ask: “Which sentence is a threat and which is a refusal? What is the only difference in the verb?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose because / to panic / to put in “Allah accepted Habil’s offering because he gave from his heart.”, “He also started to panic.” and “It showed Qabil the way to put …”, then report “I killed my brother.” and “Now I don’t know what I should do …”.
Likely errors: *because of he gave · *started panic · *the way for put · *did not know what should he do · worse where worst is needed.
Use (Activity 4): four sentences about someone who makes a serious mistake in a neutral, non-violent situation and must decide the next step.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Contrast will and won’t in a calm voice, without performing the threat: “I WON’T FIGHT BACK | and HARM you.” — won’t /wəʊnt/ is not want /wɒnt/.
Habil’s reasons in two calm chunks: “You are my BROther, | and I FEAR alLAH.”
Comparatives: “the WORST THING in LIFE” / “WORSE than this RAven”.
Read the whole chapter in a low, even voice.
Word focus: RA-ven, PAN-ic, OF-fer-ing, DIG-ging, AN-ger.
beforeReading: Set the class rule: We read this chapter calmly, we do not act it out, and we focus on choices. Retrieve from Chapter 10 how the two brothers were different.
duringReading: Lesson 1, first listening: What does Habil answer when he hears the threat?
Order six calm event cards: Offering accepted → anger → Habil’s refusal → the killing → sadness and panic → the raven.
Label each spoken sentence with its speaker.
Bridge note: the turning point + one quoted phrase + one question.
afterReading: Lesson 1: Quick Challenge with calm, text-based justification.
Lesson 2: retrieve the bridge note, then Language Focus: future / past / now (Activity 1), reason, beginning and guidance (Activity 2), reporting Qabil’s words (Activity 3).
Write two safe steps for stopping an argument before anger controls action.
content.lessonPlan: Lesson 1 (40 min): 0–5 Class rule (calm reading, no acting) and retrieval of the brothers’ differences from Chapter 10; 5–15 Teacher or audio reads once while learners listen with books closed for one question (What does Habil answer?), then read along; 15–24 Event cards in pairs: Six cards in order, each with a quoted phrase, plus speaker labels for the spoken lines; 24–31 Threat vs refusal: Pairs compare the two spoken lines and write what Habil refuses and why (You are my brother, and I fear Allah); 31–36 Quick Challenge; 36–40 Bridge note: turning point + evidence + question; Lesson 2 (40 min): 0–4 Retrieve the bridge notes; 4–13 Language Focus Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (What is the only difference between the threat and the refusal?); 13–21 Activities 2–3 in pairs, then learners explain the statement order in “what he should do”; 21–28 Raven check: One sentence about what the raven did and one about what Qabil realized (I am worse than this raven); 28–36 Use: A neutral situation (a broken school item, a serious argument between friends) in four sentences with because, won’t, didn’t know what to do and showed … the way to; 36–38 Safe steps: Pairs write two steps for stopping an argument; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Where is the turning point of the chapter?
How is Habil’s refusal different from Qabil’s threat, and what reasons does Habil give?
What does the raven do, and what does Qabil realize about himself?
What safe action can stop an argument before anger controls it?
interactiveTips: Open The Conflict hotspot only after the event order is clear, and use The Raven hotspot for what the raven showed Qabil.
Replay the threat and the refusal separately and without performance, then ask which verb changes.
Start Lesson 2 from the bridge note rather than rereading the whole scene.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Six event cards and the frames “Habil said that he ____ because ____.”, “Qabil admitted that he ____.”, “The raven showed Qabil the way to ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write eight analytical sentences about anger, refusal, consequence and regret, with reported speech (admitted that …, did not know what …) and one comparison.

formativeAssessment: Orders the events calmly and without extra detail.
Attributes each spoken line to its speaker and names threat vs refusal.
Reports words with backshift and statement order.
Proposes a safe prevention step.
expectedResponses: Allah accepted Habil’s offering because he gave from his heart; Qabil threatened him, but Habil refused to fight back because Qabil was his brother and he feared Allah. Qabil killed him, then felt very sad and started to panic, and a raven showed him the way to put his brother’s body in the pit.
content.transferTask: Write two steps for stopping an argument before anger controls action.
content.teacherReflection: Did the two-lesson split protect both comprehension and a calm atmosphere, and did learners find the will / won’t contrast themselves?

classroomManagement.instructions: Lesson 1: In pairs, put the six event cards in order and label who says each spoken line. Read quietly, and do not act out the story.
checkQuestions: Do we act out this chapter? (no)
What do you label? (who says each spoken line)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Keep the room calm and stay close to pairs who linger on violent detail. In Lesson 2, listen for statement order in “what he should do”. Check that every safe-steps list has two practical steps.

exitTicket: Write one sentence reporting Habil’s refusal (Habil said that he …) and one safe step for stopping an argument.

rubricLevels.secure: Orders the events calmly and names the speaker of each line.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the first and last cards.

rubricLevels.secure: Says the only difference between the threat and the refusal.
rubricLevels.notYet: Write the two lines one above the other and ask what changes.

rubricLevels.secure: Reports words with backshift and statement order.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “He didn’t know what he should …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Proposes one safe step to stop an argument.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Who can you ask for help?”.

interculturalFocus.notice: The raven shows Qabil how to bury his brother. Respect for the dead is a value in every culture, with different customs.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask a general question only: Which animals appear as teachers or messengers in stories from different cultures (the raven, the hoopoe, the fox)?
interculturalFocus.perspective: This chapter is sad. Avoid personal questions about death or funerals; keep the comparison to animals in stories and to the idea of respect.

content.chapter: Chapter 12: The Legacy of Adam
objectives: Synthesise the book’s lessons: Stay away from jealousy, control anger, admit mistakes and turn back to Allah, do good and avoid evil, and guidance that continues.
Distinguish events (Adam lost both sons, got old, his children spread his message) from the writer’s interpretation (The story suggests that …).
Discover how the story suggests that … should, had to, over the years, still, never, a parallel to-list and the importance of + -ing are used.
Prepare for the review pages that follow the story.
content.pedagogy: Learners test a hypothesis (three earlier chapters the ending will revisit), then build a synthesis map with four headings, linking each lesson in Chapter 12 to an earlier chapter with a quoted phrase. The Language Focus begins with one question: “Is this sentence an event on that day, or a lesson the writer takes from the story?” Learners find that “The story suggests that … should …” marks interpretation and advice. Personal application is written last and labelled as the learner’s own.
priorKnowledge: Key events of Chapters 1–11; should for advice; still.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The legacy is not only the story of the two sons: The chapter adds admitting mistakes, turning back to Allah and continuing guidance. “He” in the first sentence refers back to Chapter 11 (Qabil); learners should infer this from the previous chapter.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: The story suggests that … should … for an interpretation and advice · had to for a past necessity (as a prophet and the father …) · over the years for slow change · still (before the main verb) for something that continues now · never (Allah never left people alone) · parallel lists (to turn away …, to do good, and to avoid evil) · the importance of + -ing (admitting … and turning back …).
Notice (Activity 1): “The story suggests that true believers should stay away from jealousy and control their anger.” Ask: “Is this an event on that day, or a lesson the writer takes from the story? Which words tell you?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Complete “… Adam (pbuh) had to continue his life. He got old over the years. … their stories still guide us.”, then correct “the importance of admit mistakes” and “to do good, and avoiding evil”.
Likely errors: Must for the past · *in the years · *their stories guide still us · *the importance of admit · mixed forms in a list (to turn …, to do …, and avoiding …).
Use (Activity 4): four sentences about a person, family, class or community whose experience leaves a useful lesson.
content.pronunciationFocus:
The interpretation frame as one chunk: “the STOry sugGESTS that | TRUE beLIEVers should STAY aWAY from JEALousy”.
Stress still for continuity: “their STOries STILL GUIDE us”.
Parallel list with an even rhythm and a fall at the end: “to TURN aWAY …, | to DO GOOD, | and to aVOID Evil↘”.
Word focus: LEG-a-cy, JEAL-ous-y, sug-GEST (/səˈdʒest/), ad-MIT-ting, world-WIDE, PROPH-ets.
beforeReading: Learners choose three earlier chapters they expect the last chapter to come back to and write the chapter numbers on a sticky note as a hypothesis to check.
duringReading: Listen: Who is “He” in the first sentence? (Infer from Chapter 11.)
Mark events in one color and the writer’s lessons in another.
Underline had to, over the years and still.
Link each lesson to an earlier chapter number.
afterReading: Quick Challenge with evidence from Chapter 12 and one earlier chapter.
Language Focus: Event or interpretation (Activity 1), necessity, time and continuity (Activity 2), parallel forms (Activity 3).
Write a six-sentence synthesis with one clearly labelled personal application.
Then follow Knowledge Check → Language Review → Vocabulary Challenge → Master Glossary Part 1 → Master Glossary Part 2 → Final Challenge.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hypothesis sticky notes: Three chapters the ending may revisit; 5–12 Listen and read, then learners check their sticky notes and say who “He” is in the first sentence; 12–20 Synthesis map in groups: Four headings (jealousy and anger / admitting mistakes / doing good / continuing guidance), each lesson from Chapter 12 linked to an earlier chapter with a quoted phrase; 20–24 Quick Challenge; 24–32 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (event or lesson?), Activities 2–3 in pairs, learners explain why “still” means the message has not stopped; 32–38 Use: Four sentences about a family, class or community whose experience leaves a useful lesson (had to, over the years, still, the importance of …ing), with the personal part labelled; 38–40 Exit ticket and a one-minute orientation to the review pages.
discussionPoints: Which sentence in the chapter is an interpretation rather than an event, and how do you know?
Which lesson needs evidence from more than one earlier chapter?
What does “still” tell us about the message and the prophets’ stories?
Which part of your answer is the story and which is your own application?
interactiveTips: Use the Adam’s Family hotspot for the events of the chapter and the Continuing Guidance hotspot for the message that still guides.
Attach an earlier chapter number to every lesson on the synthesis map.
Do not treat the review pages as story chapters.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Four synthesis headings and the frames “The story suggests that we should ____.”, “Over the years, ____.”, “The message still ____.”, “It teaches the importance of ____ing.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write eight sentences using evidence from at least four earlier chapters, a parallel to-list and one “the importance of + -ing” phrase.

formativeAssessment: Separates event from interpretation.
Links final lessons to earlier chapters.
Uses had to, over the years, still and parallel forms accurately.
Labels personal application.
expectedResponses: Adam lost both of his sons on the same day and became very sad, but as a prophet and a father he had to continue his life; the story suggests that true believers should stay away from jealousy and control their anger, and the message still calls people to do good and avoid evil and teaches the importance of admitting mistakes and turning back to Allah.
content.transferTask: Describe a lesson from a family, class or community experience that still matters today and one action it suggests.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners synthesise across the book and keep the writer’s interpretation, the events and their own application clearly apart?

classroomManagement.instructions: In groups, make a synthesis map with four headings. Link each lesson from Chapter 12 to an earlier chapter with a quoted phrase.
checkQuestions: How many headings? (four)
What do you add for each lesson? (an earlier chapter and a quoted phrase)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that each lesson is linked to the right earlier chapter, for example admitting mistakes to Chapter 7. Listen for still and ask a group why it is used. In the Use task, check that personal parts are labelled.

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “still” and one “The story suggests that … should …” sentence about a story you know.

rubricLevels.secure: Links each final lesson to an earlier chapter with a quote.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the four earlier chapter numbers as a choice.

rubricLevels.secure: Says which sentences are events and which are the story’s lesson.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Did this happen, or is it what we learn?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses had to, over the years, still and parallel forms accurately.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give one gap sentence for each.

rubricLevels.secure: Labels his or her own application clearly.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “In my life, …”.

interculturalFocus.notice: The chapter says the message 'still' continues today. Every culture keeps a legacy through stories, sayings and family values.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: What is one lesson that your family or town passes on? Do you know an English-speaking person (a writer, a scientist) whose legacy continues?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners notice that legacies cross borders: an idea from one culture can help people in another. They name one such idea.

metadata.title: Teacher Guide — Prophet Adam (B1)
metadata.subtitle: TYMM-aligned guide with chapter-specific support, inductive grammar and 40-minute lesson plans
metadata.estimatedDuration: 12 chapter units: Chapters 1–10 and 12 are planned for 40 minutes; Chapter 11 is planned as 40 + 40 minutes. Review and assessment pages follow separately.
metadata.targetAudience: B1 English learners, especially lower- and upper-secondary students.
metadata.targetLearners: Learners who can follow a connected narrative, trace cause, contrast, purpose, viewpoint and consequence, and produce short evidence-based explanations.
metadata.purpose: Develop evidence-based B1 reading, listening, speaking and writing through the story of Prophet Adam (pbuh), using the Language Focus attached to every story chapter and connected production about the learners’ own world.
metadata.approachDesc: Every story chapter follows the TYMM route. YDAB1 listening and YDAB2 reading establish meaning and evidence; the Quick Challenge checks comprehension. Grammar is then learned inductively, as the Maarif Model expects for English: in the Language Focus, learners first NOTICE a form in a real chapter sentence and work out what it does (the rule is confirmed only after they formulate it), then BUILD it in controlled, meaningful practice, and finally USE it in connected YDAB3 speaking and YDAB4 writing about their own world. The story’s sensitive chapters (6 and 11) are handled calmly and non-graphically, and Chapter 11 is divided into two 40-minute lessons. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/yabanci-dil-alan-becerileri.
metadata.assessmentEvidence: 12 Quick Challenges, text-evidence checks, chapter Language Focus tasks and connected production, exit tickets, Knowledge Check, Language Review, Vocabulary Challenge and Final Challenge.

formative: Language Focus: Noticing and controlled practice

readingFramework.before: Activate only what the chapter needs, with a short chapter-specific prediction, image, question or card task.
readingFramework.during: Listen first for gist, then read and follow the chapter’s own evidence structure: time frame, cause chain, voice, sequence, contrast, role change or synthesis.
readingFramework.after: Complete the Quick Challenge, then the chapter’s Language Focus (notice → build → use), then a connected B1 transfer about the learners’ own world. In Chapter 11, Lesson 1 secures meaning and evidence and Lesson 2 develops language and production.

vocabularyApproach.selection: Prioritise chapter Word Notes and the words needed for the chapter’s key relationship.
vocabularyApproach.method: Infer meaning from context, image or audio before any direct explanation.
vocabularyApproach.recycling: Reuse vocabulary in Language Focus production, exit tickets and the review pages.

metadata.grammarApproach: Inductive and text-based. Start from the story sentence, ask a meaning question (What does this form tell us? What happened first? Whose view is it?), let learners formulate the rule in their own words, then confirm it and practise it in context. Rule explanations appear in the app only after learners answer. Do not replace the chapter work with unrelated grammar drills.
grammarSequence: Ch1: present facts vs past events; after + past; told vs said; would / was going to; said He had decided; began to
Ch2: after + have + past participle; to + verb for purpose; later; more … than; that’s why / because / so
Ch3: thought / believed / said vs narrator statements; more … than; superior to; however / but; “, which made …”
Ch4: past perfect (had put); continued + -ing; want + person + to; because of + noun; wait for a chance to; keep … away from
Ch5: key phrases (called, to be, pretending to be); start / begin + to / -ing; ask … not to; reported if … would vs direct if … will
Ch6: eventually + managed to; convinced … to; had given; time order and when-clauses; so / to / because
Ch7: key phrases (on purpose, learn from, pardon); but vs on the other hand; because; decide never to; want + person + to; to + verb
Ch8: to / for for purpose, with for means, for + period; would; had to; in addition; both … and; want + person + not to
Ch9: stop + -ing vs stop + to; time markers; became; teach + person + to; to + verb; if + present for a general truth
Ch10: key phrases (grew up to be, just a handful of); became; had to; best / healthiest; loved + -ing; but; care about + -ing
Ch11: will vs won’t; past for admission, present for judgment; worse / worst; because; start to; show … the way to; reported speech
Ch12: the story suggests that … should; had to; over the years; still; never; parallel lists; the importance of + -ing

skillsFocus.listening: TYMM YDAB1: follow narration and spoken words for gist, sequence, speaker and key details.
skillsFocus.reading: TYMM YDAB2: identify main ideas, direct evidence, character vs narrator voice, cause-result chains, contrast and interpretation.
skillsFocus.speaking: TYMM YDAB3: explain relationships, compare responses, attribute viewpoints and justify claims respectfully.
skillsFocus.writing: TYMM YDAB4: produce connected B1 paragraphs using evidence, chapter patterns and a clearly labelled personal application.

valuesFocus: D5 Sensitivity — calm, respectful handling of conflict and loss
D6 Honesty — admitting mistakes and keeping claims attributed
D9 Compassion — non-harm and care for the weak
D10 Humility — rejecting arrogance and superiority by origin
D14 Respect — respect for human diversity
D16 Responsibility — work, care for nature and repair after a mistake
D20 Helpfulness — helping the weak and the community
languageFocus: All 12 story chapters have an active Language Focus set built as notice → build → use.
Use Language Focus after basic comprehension and the Quick Challenge.
Always start from the story sentence: Ask what the form does (or whose view it is) before naming it.
Let learners answer first; the explanation shown after each answer confirms the rule they have found.
At B1 the last step is always connected production about the learners’ own world, not a retelling of the chapter.
After Chapter 12, follow Knowledge Check → Language Review → Vocabulary Challenge → Master Glossary Part 1 → Master Glossary Part 2 → Final Challenge.
metadata.differentiationNotes: Reduce linguistic load without lowering the reasoning target: One evidence sentence at a time, selected vocabulary, audio replay, sentence frames and oral rehearsal. Extend by combining more chapter patterns or adding a second evidence relationship, not by introducing outside facts.

sensitiveNotes.title: Source fidelity and respectful discussion
notes: Keep religious content within the wording of the story; do not add details, legends or explanations from outside this B1 book.

Qur’anic references, prophetic sayings, prayers and quoted words of Allah (for example Allah’s words to the angels, Adam’s plea for forgiveness) are read, explained and matched to meanings; they are never gapped, “corrected” or rewritten.
Prophets are never role-played or shown in freeze-frames; spoken lines are read calmly as reported speech.
Keep character claims separate from the narrator’s statements (Iblis in Chapters 3–5).
Chapter 2 explains different skin colors without ranking them; reject any comment that ranks people by color, origin or group (Chapter 3).
Chapter 6: treat the covering and modesty (haya) briefly, factually and non-graphically.
Chapter 11: calm, non-graphic reading, no re-enactment of the threat or the killing; the focus is on choices and prevention.
Do not present learners’ transfer sentences as new religious facts.

globalCitizenship.title: Global Citizenship and Cultural Bridges
globalCitizenship.description: The story of Adam (pbuh), the father of all humans, raises questions every community shares: How we treat people who look different from us, how we respond to our own mistakes, how we care for the earth and the weak, and how we stop anger before it causes harm.

themes.title: One human family:
themes.description: Chapter 2 explains different skin colors by soil from different parts of the earth, and Chapter 3 says greatness does not come from race, color or group. Discuss how this can shape the way we treat classmates and people from other countries.

themes.title: Admitting mistakes:
themes.description: Chapter 7 contrasts learning from a mistake with arrogance that never admits it. Discuss why admitting mistakes builds trust in teams, schools and communities.

themes.title: Caring for the earth and the weak:
themes.description: Chapter 8 names protecting nature and helping the weak as part of the human role on earth. Connect this with local environmental and volunteering projects.

themes.title: Stopping anger before harm:
themes.description: Chapters 10–11 show jealousy and anger leading to harm, and Habil refusing to fight back; Chapter 12 advises controlling anger. Discuss peaceful ways to solve disagreements at school and online.

actions: Make a class poster “One human family” with one sentence from Chapter 2 or 3 and three ways to treat everyone fairly.
Plan one small action for nature or for someone who needs help (a school clean-up, a visit to an older neighbor) and report it in four sentences.
Agree on three class steps for calming an argument before it grows.

exitTicket: One idea from today’s chapter, with the sentence that supports it, is …
One language pattern I noticed today, and what it does in the sentence, is …
One action I can take this week that shows a value from the chapter (respect, responsibility, humility, controlling anger) is …

miniProject.title: Lessons That Still Guide Us
miniProject.desc: In groups, choose one lesson from Chapter 12 (staying away from jealousy, controlling anger, admitting mistakes, doing good). Make a one-page poster or a short audio clip in clear English: Quote the sentence from the book, link it to an earlier chapter (for example Chapter 7 or Chapter 11), explain what it means, and give two realistic school examples. Use at least two Language Focus patterns such as “decided never to …”, “the importance of + -ing” or “still”.

reflectivePrompt.title: After a Mistake
reflectivePrompt.desc: Adam and Eve said sorry, learned from their mistake and decided never to repeat it; Iblis never admitted he was wrong because he was arrogant. Write six to eight sentences about a time when you or someone you know admitted a mistake at school or at home. What happened, what did you learn, and what did you decide to do differently?

valuesEducation.title: TYMM Values in Action
valuesEducation.description: Use only values genuinely supported by the chapter. Require evidence first, then connect the value to an observable, age-appropriate action. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/erdem-deger-eylem-cercevesi.

items.label: D14 Respect / D10 Humility
items.value: Reject superiority by origin, color or group (Chapters 2–3) and practise fair treatment.

items.label: D6 Honesty / D16 Responsibility
items.value: Admit mistakes, learn from them and decide what to do next (Chapters 7 and 12).

items.label: D5 Sensitivity / D20 Helpfulness
items.value: Care for nature and help the weak (Chapter 8).

items.label: D12 Patience / D9 Compassion
items.value: Control anger and refuse to harm (Chapters 11–12).
