cefrProfile.intro: This book is written for CEFR B1. The table links the B1 descriptors of the End-of-Level Test B1 to the chapters of this book where learners practise them.

rows.descriptor: Can read straightforward factual texts on subjects related to his/her field and interest with a satisfactory level of comprehension.
practice: Chapter 2 (The Shaping of Adam): Fill the three evidence rows with quoted phrases.
Chapter 6 (Satan’s Lies and Adam’s Departure from Paradise): Add the events to the timeline under the warning.
Whole book: Knowledge Check and Final Challenge.

rows.descriptor: Can write straightforward connected texts on a range of familiar subjects within his field of interest, by linking a series of shorter discrete elements into a linear sequence.
practice: Chapter 2 (The Shaping of Adam): Write four sentences about a new learning situation with one reason–result link and one comparison.
Chapter 9 (The First Messenger and the Path of Guidance): Write four sentences about someone who began guiding a group (a team captain, a club leader) and kept doing it.
Language Review, “Use: A Mistake Put Right”: Write 5–6 sentences about a mistake you put right. Tell a partner first.

rows.descriptor: Can reasonably fluently sustain a straightforward description of one of a variety of subjects within his/her field of interest, presenting it as a linear sequence of points.
practice: Chapter 2 (The Shaping of Adam): Explain one way your class can show respect to people from different places, using one reason and one result.
Chapter 9 (The First Messenger and the Path of Guidance): Describe someone who began guiding a group and never stopped doing it.
Language Review, “Use: A Mistake Put Right”: Write 5–6 sentences about a mistake you put right. Tell a partner first.

test.title: End-of-Level Test B1
test.when: Give the test when the class has finished the B1 books it reads this term. It has four parts and takes about 70 minutes plus a short speaking test for each learner.
parts: Reading and Language (45 minutes): in the app. The learner gets a test code at the end.
Writing (25 minutes): on paper. Write an article for your school website about a person you admire. (100–130 words)
Speaking (about 8 minutes): one learner with the teacher, in 2 parts.
Scoring: type the test code in “Score a test”, then score Writing and Speaking with the bands. Copy the pilot line for the pilot results sheet.

professionalDevelopment.intro: Use these steps to plan your own development with this book: rate yourself on the EPG areas with this book’s chapters, let a colleague observe one of two lessons, keep a short log after each chapter, run one small classroom enquiry, work with colleagues, and agree on scoring before the End-of-Level Test.

peerObservation.focus: Trace the chain: Iblis continues his claim → he is sent away → anger and hatred → blame → waiting for a chance → Allah’s warning to Adam.
lookFor: Instruction: In groups of three, put the six chain cards in order. Back each card with a quoted phrase. Mark where blame starts and where the warning comes.
Check questions: What do you mark on the chain? (where blame starts and where the warning comes) / Does every card need a phrase from the text? (yes)

While learners work: Give each group member one job: reader, card holder, checker. Check that the warning to be careful of Iblis is at the end of the chain. Listen for “had put” in the class discussion and ask one group why the earlier past is needed.
Evidence of “Chain order”: Orders the stages and puts the warning at the end.

peerObservation.chapter: Chapter 9: The First Messenger and the Path of Guidance
peerObservation.focus: Explain how Adam’s role develops when a community forms.
lookFor: Instruction: In pairs, match the four time phrases to their sentences from memory. Then check them in the text.
Check questions: Do you look at the text first? (no, from memory first) / How many time phrases? (four)

While learners work: Watch the race and note phrases most pairs miss, then go back to them in the class check. Listen for stop + -ing and stop + to in Activity 1. Ask two volunteers to read their guidance paragraph and the class to name the time markers.
Evidence of “Role development”: Explains how Adam became the first Messenger with evidence.

reflectionLog: After each chapter, answer the chapter’s “After the lesson” question in one or two sentences.
Write down the rubric criterion that most learners had not yet reached and the support you gave.
Every three or four chapters, look at the grammar sequence of this book and plan one short recycling activity for a form learners still avoid.
Before the End-of-Level Test, read your notes and choose two chapters to revise with the class.
standardisation: Before scoring, read the B1 descriptors for written and spoken production in the CEFR table of this book.

With a colleague, score the same three writing papers on your own with the B1 writing bands (Task, Organisation, Grammar, Vocabulary). Then compare and talk about any criterion where your scores differ by more than one band.
Score one speaking test together in the same way: both listen, both score, then compare.
Keep one agreed paper for each band as a sample for later scoring.

selfAssessment.prompt: Chapter 3: Could learners do this by the end of the lesson: “Separate the characters’ views (thought, believed, said) from the narrator’s own statements”? Which stage of the lesson flow helped most, and which did not?
Chapter 4 is planned for 40 minutes. Which stage took longer than planned, and what did you move to the next lesson?
Before the pair or group work in Chapter 6, did you ask “Where does the warning go?” How many learners could answer before they started?
In Chapter 12, how many learners were secure on “Cross-chapter evidence”? What did you do for those who were not yet secure?

When you asked “How do people in Konya protect the weak today (neighbours, kermes, food banks)?” in Chapter 8, did learners describe other cultures with facts or with stereotypes? Which words did you give them?

Which of the likely errors listed for Chapter 9 did you hear (*never stopped to send · *teaching people live · *for show · *if people will forget)? Did you correct them during the activity or after it, and why?
Which app tools did your learners use with this book (audio, Word Notes, the exercises and their result codes)? Which one gave you the most useful information about their learning?
Read your reflection log for this book. What is one change you will make the next time you teach this book, and who will you share it with?

actionResearch.question: Do learners use the past perfect for an earlier event (Chapter 4: had put, Chapter 6: had given) when they tell a story, or only in gap-fill tasks?
steps: Baseline: in the Chapter 4 transfer task, count the scenarios where the past perfect is used for an earlier event.
Recycle: in Chapters 6 and 11, ask learners to mark the earlier event in their own story with had + past participle.
Check: after the B1 End-of-Level Test, note item 13 (past perfect) for the class in Score a test, and look at the writing papers for past perfect use.
Decide: compare gap-fill and free writing results, and plan one more speaking practice for the form.

collaboration: Share your counts for past perfect with another English teacher who uses this book, and agree on one activity to try in both classes.
Plan the Chapter 2 discussion on difference and respect with the religious culture teacher, so both lessons use the same examples.

content.chapter: Chapter 1: Introduction & The Creation
objectives: I can explain who Adam (pbuh) is and how the Holy Qur’an tells his story.
I can explain what Allah told the angels and how they reacted.
I can separate facts that are true now from events that happened in the story.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Sort parts of the chapter into what is true now (is, tells, can learn) and what happened in the story (created, gave, were surprised), complete the lines with After, told and would, then fix two mistakes: had decided in reported speech, and began to wait.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: MES-sen-ger, FAB-u-lous, RUL-er, cu-ri-OS-i-ty. Make a small pause after “After Allah created the sky and the earth”, then go on with “He told the angels”.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, look at the two hotspots. What does a ruler on earth have to do? Listen once for the main idea: Who is Adam (pbuh), and what did Allah announce? Read paragraph 1 again and mark the present verbs (is, tells, can learn). Then mark the past verbs in paragraph 2.
discussionPoints: Allah placed a ruler (khalifah) on earth, a person given responsibility. What is one responsibility you have at home or at school, and how do you take care of it?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Created from Soil” and “Responsibility on Earth”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to the end of paragraph 2. Read the last sentence and find two things the angels did. Check each option: Does it belong to the angels, and does it happen in this chapter? Then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences. Start with a fact that is true now about a source (a book, a website, a teacher), move into past events with after and told, and end with something that was going to happen or would happen later.

whatToNotice: The chapter has two parts: Paragraph 1 introduces Adam (pbuh) and the sources of his story, and paragraph 2 tells the first event.
Notice “This ruler would live there for many years.” Would looks forward from a past moment: The ruler was not on earth yet.
readListen: Before you read, look at the two hotspots. What does a ruler on earth have to do?
Listen once for the main idea: Who is Adam (pbuh), and what did Allah announce?
Read paragraph 1 again and mark the present verbs (is, tells, can learn). Then mark the past verbs in paragraph 2.
Open the picture hotspots “Created from Soil” and “Responsibility on Earth” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find two things Allah gave Adam (pbuh) as the first human, and the surahs that tell his tale.
Paragraph 1: find what we can learn from this story and what its messages are about.
Paragraph 2: find what Allah told the angels and what He had decided.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: messenger, fabulous, ruler, curiosity.
“He said He had decided to place a ruler (khalifah) on earth.” What does a ruler do, according to the Word Note?
Use curiosity in one sentence about something you waited to find out.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks how the angels reacted to Allah’s news. The answer is in the last sentence of paragraph 2. Remember that Adam (pbuh) is not created yet in this chapter.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to the end of paragraph 2.
Read the last sentence and find two things the angels did.
Check each option: Does it belong to the angels, and does it happen in this chapter? Then try again.
selfCheck: Can I say who Adam (pbuh) is with two facts?
Can I explain what the ruler (khalifah) would do?
Can I tell a present fact from a past event in this chapter?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences. Start with a fact that is true now about a source (a book, a website, a teacher), move into past events with after and told, and end with something that was going to happen or would happen later.
content.reflectionPrompt: Allah placed a ruler (khalifah) on earth, a person given responsibility. What is one responsibility you have at home or at school, and how do you take care of it?

content.chapter: Chapter 2: The Shaping of Adam
objectives: I can explain why humans have different skin colors, using evidence from the chapter.
I can explain what Allah gave Adam (pbuh) and why.
I can show the same cause and result with That’s why, because and so.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Decide when the angels were to show respect (After I have created …), complete the lines with to, Later and than, then say the soil-and-skin-color link in two new ways: Result first with because, and reason first with so or which is why.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: IN-tel-lect, KNOWL-edge, HAND-ful, SHAPED (one syllable). The k in knowledge is silent. Stress the compared words in “more knowledge than the angels”.
content.lessonPlan: Look at both hotspots. What do soil and knowledge have to do with being human? Listen once and follow the text. Read the chapter again and draw three arrows: One in paragraph 1 and two in paragraph 2.
discussionPoints: The chapter says people have different skin colors because the soil came from different lands. How can this idea help people treat each other fairly?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Soil from Many Lands” and “A Gift of Knowledge”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 1 and find “That’s why”. What does it point back to? In paragraph 2, read the words after “life and intellect” and after “He taught Adam (pbuh)”. Keep three separate arrows, then match again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about a new learning situation. Report what a teacher said, explain a reason and a result with so or that’s why, give a purpose with to, and finish with a more … than comparison.

whatToNotice: The chapter gives three links: Soil from different lands → different skin colors; life and intellect → learning and understanding; Allah’s teaching → doing good on earth.
Notice “After I have created Adam (pbuh) and given him life and knowledge, show respect to him.” The respect comes only after the creation is complete.
readListen: Look at both hotspots. What do soil and knowledge have to do with being human?
Listen once and follow the text.
Read the chapter again and draw three arrows: One in paragraph 1 and two in paragraph 2.
Open the picture hotspots “Soil from Many Lands” and “A Gift of Knowledge” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find where the soil came from and the sentence that starts with “That’s why”.
Paragraph 1: find what Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) said about the children of Adam (pbuh).
Paragraph 2: find the purpose of life and intellect, what Allah taught Adam (pbuh), and the comparison with the angels.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: handful, intellect, knowledge, shaped.
“a handful of dust from different lands”: How much dust is a handful?
Write one sentence with intellect and one with knowledge about how you learn.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will match three gifts or actions with their results. The first link is in paragraph 1 and the other two are in paragraph 2. Follow the linking words.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 1 and find “That’s why”. What does it point back to?
In paragraph 2, read the words after “life and intellect” and after “He taught Adam (pbuh)”.
Keep three separate arrows, then match again.
selfCheck: Can I explain all three links without mixing them?
Can I say why the angels had to wait before showing respect?
Can I say the same cause and result with because and with so?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about a new learning situation. Report what a teacher said, explain a reason and a result with so or that’s why, give a purpose with to, and finish with a more … than comparison.
content.reflectionPrompt: The chapter says people have different skin colors because the soil came from different lands. How can this idea help people treat each other fairly?

content.chapter: Chapter 3: Iblis’s Arrogance
objectives: I can explain why Iblis thought he was better than Adam (pbuh).
I can explain, with evidence, why the narrator says Iblis was wrong.
I can separate a character’s view from the narrator’s own statement.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Sort parts of the chapter into a character’s view (thought, believed, said) and the narrator’s own statement, choose more important, superior to and However, then fix three mistakes: Adam was after thought that, but for the opposite reaction, and which for a comment on the idea before it.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: AR-ro-gant, OR-i-gin, su-pe-ri-OR-i-ty, ad-MIRED. Stress the compared words in “I am better than Adam (pbuh).” and pause after However.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the Fire and Soil hotspot. What did Iblis compare? Listen once and follow the text. Read paragraph 2 again and mark what Iblis believed and what the narrator says.
discussionPoints: The chapter says greatness does not come from race, color or group. Why do people sometimes judge others by where they come from, and what should we look at instead?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Fire and Soil” and “Equal in Allah’s Sight”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 2. Read the sentence with “couldn’t see and accept” to the end, then the sentence that starts with However. Remove any option that only repeats Iblis’s own view, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about a new situation with two different opinions. Report both views with thought that or believed, add a reason with because, compare with better than or more … than, and give your conclusion with but or however.

whatToNotice: The angels and Iblis look at the same being but react in opposite ways. The word but in paragraph 1 marks the contrast.
Notice “Iblis thought that Adam was an unimportant being created from clay.” Thought that tells us this is Iblis’s view, not the truth.
readListen: Look at the Fire and Soil hotspot. What did Iblis compare?
Listen once and follow the text.
Read paragraph 2 again and mark what Iblis believed and what the narrator says.
Open the picture hotspots “Fire and Soil” and “Equal in Allah’s Sight” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find how the angels reacted to Adam (pbuh) and what Iblis thought instead.
Paragraph 1: find Iblis’s answer to Allah’s question and the reason he gave.
Paragraph 2: find what Iblis could not see, and the sentence that starts with However.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: admired, arrogant, origin, superiority.
“he believed his origin was superior”: What was his origin, and why did he think it mattered?
Write one sentence with admired and one with arrogant.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why Iblis was wrong. Compare what he says about fire and soil in paragraph 1 with paragraph 2, where the narrator says what he could not see.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 2.
Read the sentence with “couldn’t see and accept” to the end, then the sentence that starts with However.
Remove any option that only repeats Iblis’s own view, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I say Iblis’s claim and his reason?
Can I give the narrator’s evidence that he was wrong?
Can I use thought that and more … than correctly?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about a new situation with two different opinions. Report both views with thought that or believed, add a reason with because, compare with better than or more … than, and give your conclusion with but or however.
content.reflectionPrompt: The chapter says greatness does not come from race, color or group. Why do people sometimes judge others by where they come from, and what should we look at instead?

content.chapter: Chapter 4: The Expulsion of Iblis
objectives: I can explain why Iblis became angry with Adam (pbuh).
I can explain what Iblis planned and how Allah protected Adam (pbuh) with a warning.
I can use the past perfect to show which past event came first.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Decide why the writer says had put and not put, choose continued saying, want Allah to be and because of, then rebuild the sentence about Iblis’s plan: He waited for a chance to keep Adam (pbuh) away from Allah’s kindness.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: CRE-a-tor, EN-e-my, CARE-ful. Warned has one syllable: /wɔːnd/. Say Allah’s command short and strong: “Go away!”
content.lessonPlan: Look at The Warning hotspot. Who warned whom? Listen once and follow the text. Read paragraph 1 again and underline what Iblis continued saying, what he felt and what he thought.
discussionPoints: Iblis blamed Adam (pbuh) instead of admitting his own mistake. Why is it easier to blame someone else, and what does it cost us?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Distance from Mercy” and “The Warning”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 1. Read what Iblis continued saying, then the sentence with “because of Adam (pbuh)”. Ask: Whom did Iblis blame? Then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about a new situation in which someone continues a harmful plan and another person gives a warning. Use continued + -ing, because of, waited for a chance to and warned … to be careful of.

whatToNotice: Iblis does not accept that he was wrong. He blames Adam (pbuh) instead, and his anger becomes a plan.
Notice “Allah had put him far from His help.” Had put shows that being sent away came before Iblis’s thought.
readListen: Look at The Warning hotspot. Who warned whom?
Listen once and follow the text.
Read paragraph 1 again and underline what Iblis continued saying, what he felt and what he thought.
Open the picture hotspots “Distance from Mercy” and “The Warning” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find what Iblis continued saying and what Allah said to him.
Paragraph 1: find whom Iblis blamed and the words “because of”.
Paragraph 2: find what Iblis waited for and what Allah told Adam (pbuh).
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: Creator, hated, enemy, careful.
“warned him to be careful of Iblis”: Why is a warning a kind of help?
Write one sentence with hated and one with careful.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The statement says Iblis blamed himself. Read paragraph 1 and find the sentence that starts with “He thought that” before you decide.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 1.
Read what Iblis continued saying, then the sentence with “because of Adam (pbuh)”.
Ask: Whom did Iblis blame? Then try again.
selfCheck: Can I explain whom Iblis blamed and why?
Can I say which came first: Allah’s words or Iblis’s thought?
Can I use continued + -ing and because of correctly?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about a new situation in which someone continues a harmful plan and another person gives a warning. Use continued + -ing, because of, waited for a chance to and warned … to be careful of.
content.reflectionPrompt: Iblis blamed Adam (pbuh) instead of admitting his own mistake. Why is it easier to blame someone else, and what does it cost us?

content.chapter: Chapter 5: Life in Paradise and the Warning
objectives: I can describe life in Paradise and explain why Allah gave Adam (pbuh) a companion.
I can explain the one rule and the lie Iblis told.
I can change reported words into direct words with if … will.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Match phrases such as “a wife called Eve (Hawwa)” and “more wonderful than we can imagine” with their meanings, choose started to feel, began living and asked them not to go, then change the reported whisper into Iblis’s direct words with if + present and will.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: LONE-ly, com-PAN-ion, BLESS-ings, pre-TEND-ing. Say the whisper in two parts: “if they ate from that one tree,” then “they would never die”.
content.lessonPlan: Look at The One Tree hotspot. Why does one tree matter in a place with so many blessings? Listen once and follow the text. Read paragraph 2 again and mark the rule, the lie and the false promise.
discussionPoints: Iblis came with a friendly face, but his words were a lie. How can you check whether someone’s friendly advice is really good for you?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “A Companion for Adam” and “The One Tree”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to the last two sentences of this chapter. Then read the first sentence of paragraph 2 in Chapter 4: what was Iblis waiting for? Ask: What did Iblis want Adam (pbuh) and Eve to do? Then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about a new situation with a beginning, one clear restriction and a conditional result. Use started to or began + -ing, asked … not to, and an if … would sentence.

whatToNotice: Paragraph 1 is full of good things (a companion, blessings). Paragraph 2 brings one rule and one danger.
Notice “pretending to be their friend” and the next sentence: “It was a big lie.” The narrator tells us plainly not to trust Iblis’s friendly face.
readListen: Look at The One Tree hotspot. Why does one tree matter in a place with so many blessings?
Listen once and follow the text.
Read paragraph 2 again and mark the rule, the lie and the false promise.
Open the picture hotspots “A Companion for Adam” and “The One Tree” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find how Adam (pbuh) felt and why Allah gave him a wife.
Paragraph 1: find how the writer compares Paradise with our imagination.
Paragraph 2: find the one thing Allah asked, and what Iblis whispered to them.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: lonely, companion, blessings, whispered.
“to be his companion”: What does a companion do for a person who feels lonely?
Write one sentence with blessings and one with whispered.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why Iblis pretended to be their friend. Read the end of paragraph 2 here, and the first sentence of paragraph 2 in Chapter 4, where Iblis waits for something.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to the last two sentences of this chapter.
Then read the first sentence of paragraph 2 in Chapter 4: what was Iblis waiting for?
Ask: What did Iblis want Adam (pbuh) and Eve to do? Then try again.
selfCheck: Can I describe Paradise and the one rule in two sentences?
Can I explain why Iblis pretended to be a friend?
Can I say Iblis’s whisper as direct words with if … will?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about a new situation with a beginning, one clear restriction and a conditional result. Use started to or began + -ing, asked … not to, and an if … would sentence.
content.reflectionPrompt: Iblis came with a friendly face, but his words were a lie. How can you check whether someone’s friendly advice is really good for you?

content.chapter: Chapter 6: Satan’s lies and Adam’s Departure from Paradise
objectives: I can put the events of the chapter in order.
I can explain how Adam (pbuh) and Eve felt after they ate from the tree.
I can explain why they covered themselves, using so, to and because.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Decide what eventually and managed to tell us together, put five events in the order they happened, then complete the lines with so (a result), to (a purpose) and because (a reason).
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: for-BID-den, VIS-i-ble, in-BORN, HAR-mo-ny. Say the list of actions with a small rise on each verb: “stretched out his hand, picked one of the fruits and offered it to Eve”.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the Modesty hotspot. What is modesty? Listen once and follow the events. Read the chapter again and number the events in your notebook.
discussionPoints: They forgot the warning Allah had given them. What helps you remember good advice at the moment you really need it?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “The Forbidden Tree” and “Modesty”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 3. Read the last sentence and find the reason after because. Remove any option that belongs to another chapter, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about a new situation in which an earlier warning is forgotten, an action causes a change, and someone reacts for a clear purpose. Use managed to, when, so, to + verb and because.

whatToNotice: The chapter is a chain: A trick → a forgotten warning → eating from the tree → pain and shame → covering themselves.
Notice “Eventually, Iblis managed to trick them.” Eventually and managed to show that Iblis tried for some time before he succeeded.
readListen: Look at the Modesty hotspot. What is modesty?
Listen once and follow the events.
Read the chapter again and number the events in your notebook.
Open the picture hotspots “The Forbidden Tree” and “Modesty” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find what Iblis did and what Adam (pbuh) and Eve forgot.
Paragraph 2: find how Adam (pbuh) felt when he finished eating and what changed around him.
Paragraph 3: find what they saw, what they did, and the word because.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: forbidden, shame, visible, inborn.
“a sense of shame (haya) is part of inborn human nature”: What does inborn tell you about haya?
Write one sentence with forbidden and one with visible.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why they hurried to cover themselves. The answer is in the last sentence of paragraph 3, after because.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 3.
Read the last sentence and find the reason after because.
Remove any option that belongs to another chapter, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I tell the events in order?
Can I describe their feelings after eating?
Can I give a result with so, a purpose with to and a reason with because?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about a new situation in which an earlier warning is forgotten, an action causes a change, and someone reacts for a clear purpose. Use managed to, when, so, to + verb and because.
content.reflectionPrompt: They forgot the warning Allah had given them. What helps you remember good advice at the moment you really need it?

content.chapter: Chapter 7: Forgiveness and Repentance
objectives: I can compare how Adam (pbuh) and Eve responded to their mistake with how Iblis responded.
I can explain why arrogance is called the biggest barrier.
I can use but, On the other hand and because to connect two responses.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Match phrases such as “learned from their mistake” and “chose an opposite path” with their meanings, complete the lines with but, On the other hand and because, then choose decided never to repeat, wanted Allah to pardon and to live.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: OP-po-site, PAR-don, BAR-ri-er, dis-TIN-guish-ing. Say Adam’s answer gently: “No, my Lord, but I am shy of You.”
content.lessonPlan: Look at the Arrogance as a Barrier hotspot. What can a barrier stop? Listen once and follow the text. Read paragraphs 2 and 3 again and make two lists: What Adam (pbuh) and Eve did, and what Iblis did.
discussionPoints: Adam (pbuh) said sorry and learned from his mistake. What makes an apology real, and why is it sometimes hard to say sorry?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Mistake and Pardon” and “Arrogance as a Barrier”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraphs 2 and 3. Find “On the other hand” and read the two sentences after it. Match again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about a new situation where someone makes a mistake that was not on purpose, responds responsibly and takes a useful next step. Use at least four patterns, such as learned from, decided never to, wanted … to, because and on the other hand.

whatToNotice: The chapter puts two paths side by side: Adam (pbuh) and Eve say sorry and learn, while Iblis never admits he was wrong.
Notice “it wasn’t on purpose”: the mistake was real, but it was not planned.
readListen: Look at the Arrogance as a Barrier hotspot. What can a barrier stop?
Listen once and follow the text.
Read paragraphs 2 and 3 again and make two lists: What Adam (pbuh) and Eve did, and what Iblis did.
Open the picture hotspots “Mistake and Pardon” and “Arrogance as a Barrier” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find what Adam (pbuh) cried and how he answered Allah’s question.
Paragraph 2: find four things Adam (pbuh) and Eve did after their mistake.
Paragraphs 3–4: find why Iblis never admitted he was wrong, and what Allah did for Adam (pbuh) and Eve.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: opposite, pardon, barrier, distinguishing.
“the biggest barrier to acting the right way”: What does arrogance stop people from doing?
Write one sentence with pardon and one with opposite.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will match Adam (pbuh) and Eve, Iblis and arrogance with what the chapter says. Use paragraph 2 for Adam (pbuh) and Eve, and paragraph 3 for Iblis and arrogance.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraphs 2 and 3.
Find “On the other hand” and read the two sentences after it.
Match again.
selfCheck: Can I describe the two paths in one sentence with on the other hand?
Can I explain why arrogance is a barrier?
Can I use decided never to and wanted … to correctly?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about a new situation where someone makes a mistake that was not on purpose, responds responsibly and takes a useful next step. Use at least four patterns, such as learned from, decided never to, wanted … to, because and on the other hand.
content.reflectionPrompt: Adam (pbuh) said sorry and learned from his mistake. What makes an apology real, and why is it sometimes hard to say sorry?

content.chapter: Chapter 8: Struggle and Survival on Earth
objectives: I can describe the work Adam (pbuh) and Eve would do on earth.
I can explain why life on earth was a struggle.
I can say why, with what and how long with to, with and for.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Sort phrases by what they add: why (to grow, for shelter), with what (with clothes and weapons) or how long (for many years), fix three mistakes (would, to survive, people not to remember), then complete the lines with In addition, had to and both.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: SHEL-ter, STRUG-gle, sur-VIVE, WEAP-ons. The ea in weapons sounds like the e in bed.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the Work on Earth hotspot. What kinds of work do you see? Listen once and follow the text. Read paragraph 2 again and list everything they had to do.
discussionPoints: Adam (pbuh) and Eve would protect nature and help the weak. What is one small way you can do these two things this week?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Work on Earth” and “Protection from Danger”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 2 of this chapter and read what they had to do. Then read about the blessings in paragraph 1 of Chapter 5. Decide if life was the same in both places, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about people who begin life in a difficult new place. Use at least four patterns: would for an expected role, had to, to + verb for purpose, in addition, with + noun, because, or for + a period of time.

whatToNotice: Paragraph 1 describes the role that was still ahead of them (would). Paragraph 2 describes what they really had to do (had to).
Notice “He was still there because he wanted people not to remember Allah.” The danger of Iblis did not end in Paradise; he followed them to earth.
readListen: Look at the Work on Earth hotspot. What kinds of work do you see?
Listen once and follow the text.
Read paragraph 2 again and list everything they had to do.
Open the picture hotspots “Work on Earth” and “Protection from Danger” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find five things they would do on earth.
Paragraph 2: find what they had to do to survive, and the words “In addition”.
Paragraph 3: find why Iblis followed them and how long Adam (pbuh) and Eve lived on earth.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: shelter, struggle, survive, weapons.
“they had to struggle to survive”: Why is this very different from life in Paradise?
Write one sentence with shelter and one with survive.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The statement compares life on earth with life in Paradise. Compare paragraph 1 of Chapter 5 with paragraph 2 of this chapter.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 2 of this chapter and read what they had to do.
Then read about the blessings in paragraph 1 of Chapter 5.
Decide if life was the same in both places, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I name three things they had to do on earth?
Can I explain why Iblis followed them?
Can I use to, with and for with the right meaning?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about people who begin life in a difficult new place. Use at least four patterns: would for an expected role, had to, to + verb for purpose, in addition, with + noun, because, or for + a period of time.
content.reflectionPrompt: Adam (pbuh) and Eve would protect nature and help the weak. What is one small way you can do these two things this week?

content.chapter: Chapter 9: The First Messenger and the Path of Guidance
objectives: I can explain when and how Adam (pbuh) became the first Messenger.
I can explain why Allah kept sending messengers.
I can follow the chapter’s time markers from the beginning to years later.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Decide if never stopped sending means the same as never stopped to send, put four parts of the chapter in order with the time markers, then fix three mistakes: teaching people to live, to show (not for show), and if people forget (not will forget).
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: com-MU-ni-ty, RIGHT-eous-ly, SA-cred, PUR-pose. Righteously sounds like RIGHT-chus-ly.
content.lessonPlan: Look at The First Community hotspot. Why does a community need a guide? Listen once and follow the text. Read the chapter again and circle At that time, After a period of time, Thus and Years later.
discussionPoints: The chapter says that if people forget Allah, they lose the meaning and purpose of life. What gives your day meaning and purpose?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “The First Community” and “Messengers and Sacred Texts”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 3. Read the last sentence from because to the end. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about someone who begins guiding a group. Use at least four patterns: after or when, became, started teaching … to, never stopped + -ing, to + verb for purpose, wanted … to, or if + present for a general result.

whatToNotice: The chapter moves through time: No community → a community and the first Messenger → many messengers after the death of Adam (pbuh).
Notice “Allah never stopped sending messengers and sacred texts to remind people of Him.” Never stopped sending means the sending went on.
readListen: Look at The First Community hotspot. Why does a community need a guide?
Listen once and follow the text.
Read the chapter again and circle At that time, After a period of time, Thus and Years later.
Open the picture hotspots “The First Community” and “Messengers and Sacred Texts” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find when Adam (pbuh) became the first Messenger and what he taught people.
Paragraph 2: find what Adam (pbuh) and Eve taught their children, and why.
Paragraph 3: find why Allah sent many other messengers and why people should keep Allah in their minds.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: community, righteously, sacred, purpose.
“to live righteously and act honestly”: What does a person who lives righteously do?
Write one sentence with community and one with purpose.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why the messengers wanted people to keep Allah in their minds. The answer is in the last sentence of paragraph 3, after because.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 3.
Read the last sentence from because to the end.
Try again.
selfCheck: Can I tell the three stages of the chapter with time markers?
Can I explain why messengers kept coming?
Can I use teach + person + to and never stopped + -ing?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about someone who begins guiding a group. Use at least four patterns: after or when, became, started teaching … to, never stopped + -ing, to + verb for purpose, wanted … to, or if + present for a general result.
content.reflectionPrompt: The chapter says that if people forget Allah, they lose the meaning and purpose of life. What gives your day meaning and purpose?

content.chapter: Chapter 10: The Two Sons: Habil and Qabil
objectives: I can describe how Habil and Qabil were different.
I can compare the two offerings and explain what they show.
I can use but, had to and best to compare and explain.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Match phrases such as “grew up to be” and “a serious disagreement” with their meanings, choose became, had to and best, then fix three mistakes: loved taking, but Qabil, and care about pleasing.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: JEAL-ous, SHEP-herd, dis-a-GREE-ment, OF-fer-ing. The h in shepherd is silent: SHEP-erd.
content.lessonPlan: Look at The Two Offerings hotspot. What did each brother bring? Listen once and follow the text. Read the chapter again and make a table: Habil / Qabil (character, work, gift).
discussionPoints: The chapter says real goodness is giving out the best and the most loved. When did someone give you their best, and how did it feel?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Two Different Brothers” and “The Two Offerings”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to paragraph 2. Read the sentence about Qabil that comes after the two gifts. Check each option against that sentence, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about two people who respond differently to the same task. Use at least four patterns: when … grew up, became, to + verb for purpose, had to, but or however, didn’t care about + -ing, and a general principle such as real responsibility is + -ing.

whatToNotice: Paragraph 1 compares the brothers’ characters and work. Paragraph 2 shows the difference in action, in their gifts.
Notice “just a handful of his crops that were not very valuable”. Just makes the gift sound small next to Habil’s best sheep.
readListen: Look at The Two Offerings hotspot. What did each brother bring?
Listen once and follow the text.
Read the chapter again and make a table: Habil / Qabil (character, work, gift).
Open the picture hotspots “Two Different Brothers” and “The Two Offerings” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Paragraph 1: find how Habil and Qabil were different in character.
Paragraph 1: find the work each brother did when they grew up.
Paragraph 2: find why they made an offering, what each one brought, and the sentence that starts with However.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: jealous, shepherd, disagreement, offering.
“Qabil was mostly jealous.” What does mostly add?
Write one sentence with disagreement and one with offering.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks what Qabil’s offering shows about him. Compare the two gifts in paragraph 2, then read the sentence that comes after them.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to paragraph 2.
Read the sentence about Qabil that comes after the two gifts.
Check each option against that sentence, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I describe both brothers in one sentence with but?
Can I explain what the two offerings show?
Can I use had to and best correctly?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about two people who respond differently to the same task. Use at least four patterns: when … grew up, became, to + verb for purpose, had to, but or however, didn’t care about + -ing, and a general principle such as real responsibility is + -ing.
content.reflectionPrompt: The chapter says real goodness is giving out the best and the most loved. When did someone give you their best, and how did it feel?

content.chapter: Chapter 11: The First Conflict and the Raven
objectives: I can put the events of the chapter in order, from the accepted offering to Qabil’s regret.
I can compare Qabil’s threat with Habil’s refusal.
I can report what someone said with admitted that and did not know what.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Sort the spoken words into the future (a threat or a refusal), the past (an admission) and now (a judgment or an inability), choose because, started to panic and the way to put, then report Qabil’s words with admitted that he had killed and did not know what he should do.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: RA-ven, PAN-ic, DIG-ging. Compare worse and worst: “I am worse than this raven” compares two things, and “the worst thing in life” compares with everything.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the A Lesson from a Bird hotspot. What did the raven show Qabil? Listen once and follow the text. The chapter describes a killing, so read it calmly and focus on the choices and feelings. Read the chapter again and mark who says each line of direct speech.
discussionPoints: Habil said he would not fight back because he feared Allah. What can a person do to stop anger before it grows?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Brother Against Brother” and “A Lesson from a Bird”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the chapter again and stop after each event. Remember that the raven comes only after Qabil does not know what to do. Put the events in order again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about someone who makes a serious mistake and then has to decide what to do next. Use at least four patterns: because, will or won’t, when, started + -ing, didn’t know what … should, showed … the way to, or worse than. Write about a new situation, not this chapter.

whatToNotice: Qabil’s anger comes first and his sadness comes later. Notice “Soon, Qabil’s anger cooled, and he felt very sad.”
The spoken words show three times: a threat and a refusal about the future, an admission about the past, and a judgment about now.
readListen: Look at the A Lesson from a Bird hotspot. What did the raven show Qabil?
Listen once and follow the text. The chapter describes a killing, so read it calmly and focus on the choices and feelings.
Read the chapter again and mark who says each line of direct speech.
Open the picture hotspots “Brother Against Brother” and “A Lesson from a Bird” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Beginning: Find why Allah accepted Habil’s offering and how Qabil reacted.
Middle: Find Habil’s answer and the two reasons he gives.
End: Find how Qabil felt after his anger cooled, what the raven did, and what Qabil said about himself.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: harm, panic, raven, digging.
“I won’t fight back and harm you.” What does Habil refuse to do?
Write one sentence with panic about a calm way to deal with it.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will put five events in order. The chapter is one paragraph: Follow it from the first sentence to the last.
wrongAnswerSupport: Read the chapter again and stop after each event.
Remember that the raven comes only after Qabil does not know what to do.
Put the events in order again.
selfCheck: Can I tell the events in order without adding details?
Can I explain the difference between Qabil’s threat and Habil’s refusal?
Can I report Qabil’s words with admitted that?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about someone who makes a serious mistake and then has to decide what to do next. Use at least four patterns: because, will or won’t, when, started + -ing, didn’t know what … should, showed … the way to, or worse than. Write about a new situation, not this chapter.
content.reflectionPrompt: Habil said he would not fight back because he feared Allah. What can a person do to stop anger before it grows?

content.chapter: Chapter 12: The Legacy of Adam
objectives: I can explain why Adam (pbuh) had to continue his life after losing his sons.
I can name the lessons the story leaves for people today.
I can use had to, over the years and still for necessity, time and continuity.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Decide what “The story suggests that” does in the sentence about jealousy and anger, complete the lines with had to, over and still, then fix two mistakes: the importance of admitting, and to avoid to keep the list parallel.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: MES-sage, ad-MIT-ting, world-WIDE, JEAL-ous-y. Stress still for continuity: “their stories still guide us”.
content.lessonPlan: Look at the A Lasting Message hotspot. What does the message still teach? Listen once and follow the text. Read the chapter again and underline every still.
discussionPoints: The message teaches the importance of admitting mistakes and turning back to Allah. Why is admitting a mistake a sign of strength, not weakness?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “A Family Across the World” and “A Lasting Message”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to the middle of the chapter. Read the sentence that starts with But, up to had to. Remove any option that belongs to Chapter 11, then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about a person, family, class or community whose experience leaves a useful lesson. Use at least four patterns: as a … had to, over the years, still, never, suggests that … should, or the importance of + -ing.

whatToNotice: The chapter moves from sadness to continuity: a loss, a duty, a family across the world and a message that still guides people.
Notice “The story suggests that true believers should stay away from jealousy and control their anger.” This is advice the writer takes from the story, not an event in it.
readListen: Look at the A Lasting Message hotspot. What does the message still teach?
Listen once and follow the text.
Read the chapter again and underline every still.
Open the picture hotspots “A Family Across the World” and “A Lasting Message” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Beginning: Find why Adam (pbuh) became very sad.
Middle: Find the sentence that starts with But, and what his children and grandchildren did.
End: Find what the message still calls people to do and what it teaches about mistakes.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: spread, admitting, message, guide.
“spread his message worldwide”: How did the message reach the whole world?
Write one sentence with admitting and one with guide.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why Adam (pbuh) still had to continue his life. Read the middle of the chapter and find the sentence that starts with But.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to the middle of the chapter.
Read the sentence that starts with But, up to had to.
Remove any option that belongs to Chapter 11, then try again.
selfCheck: Can I explain the two roles of Adam (pbuh) in one sentence?
Can I name two lessons the message still teaches?
Can I use had to, over the years and still correctly?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say four connected sentences about a person, family, class or community whose experience leaves a useful lesson. Use at least four patterns: as a … had to, over the years, still, never, suggests that … should, or the importance of + -ing.
content.reflectionPrompt: The message teaches the importance of admitting mistakes and turning back to Allah. Why is admitting a mistake a sign of strength, not weakness?

metadata.whoIsThisFor: B1 learners who study the story of Prophet Adam (pbuh) on their own or at home.
learningGoals: Understand the 12 chapters of the story of Prophet Adam (pbuh).
Find evidence in the story before answering.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in connected sentences.
Connect humility, responsibility and self-control with real actions.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Listen and read before the Quick Challenge.
Repair wrong answers with the text.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 12.

sections.title: 1. One Chapter per Session
sections.text: Each chapter takes about 25 minutes. Open “Study Path” for the steps of your chapter.
points: Preview the title and hotspots.
Listen and read for the main idea.
Find the evidence.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 2. Listen and Read
sections.text: Use the audio twice: Once for the main idea, once to follow the exact words.
points: First listening: What is the chapter about?
Second listening: Follow the text line by line.
Replay one long sentence and say it with the same pauses.

sections.title: 3. Word Notes and Hotspots
sections.text: Each chapter has four Word Notes and two picture hotspots. Use them after you have tried to understand the sentence yourself.
points: Guess the meaning from the sentence.
Check the Word Note.
Write the word in a new sentence of your own.

sections.title: 4. Quick Challenge
sections.text: Answer before you read the feedback. If you are wrong, repair the answer with the text.
points: Find the paragraph the question is about.
Read the key sentence again.
Explain why the right answer is right, then try again.

sections.title: 5. Language Focus
sections.text: Each chapter has four Language Focus activities built from the chapter’s own sentences.
points: Activity 1 (Notice): Look at a sentence and what it means.
Activities 2–3 (Build): choose, complete, correct or rewrite forms.
Activity 4 (Use): Write or say four connected sentences about a new situation.

sections.title: 6. When It Is Hard
sections.text: Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Work one paragraph at a time.
Use the hotspots to get the big picture first.
Write a one-line summary of each paragraph.
Focus on two Word Notes today.

sections.title: 7. Values in the Story
sections.text: The book contrasts arrogance and jealousy with humility, repentance and good action. Connect each value to one action.
points: Humility: Value comes from knowledge and goodness, not from origin, race or color (Chapter 3).
Responsibility: Admit your mistake, say sorry and learn from it instead of blaming others (Chapters 4, 7 and 12).
Care with trust: Check friendly words before you believe them (Chapters 5 and 6).
Generosity: Give your best, not what is left over (Chapter 10).
Self-control: Stop jealousy and anger before they grow (Chapters 11 and 12).

sections.title: 8. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 12, do the review pages in this order. Go back to the chapter when an answer is not clear.
points: Knowledge Check
Master Glossary
Vocabulary Challenge
Language Review
Final Challenge
